translation_en:
…kings were in their love for the people and how far-reaching in their consideration of affairs. Even so, guiding the people does not rely solely on words, and defending the state does not depend merely on strategic terrain. That King Kang commanded the Duke of Bi to protect and regulate, and followed it by saying, "Only virtue, only righteousness," was truly for good reason!

Classic of Poetry (Shijing)
"We are utterly exhausted, yet we have performed the rites without fault. The able invoker conveys the announcement, going to present it to the filial descendant: 'Fragrant is your filial sacrifice; the spirits delight in your drink and food. They foretell for you a hundred blessings, according to the due time, according to the due measure. You have been reverent, you have been expeditious; you have been upright, you have been cautious. Forever they will bestow on you the utmost blessings, in tens of thousands, in hundreds of millions.'"
Ye Bingjing 葉秉敬

Associate Examiner, County Director of Studies Chen, comments: Stripping away all superficial verbiage, from beginning to end it emphasizes the single word "reverence," capturing the intent of the poet.
Associate Examiner, County Director of Studies Chen, comments: The structure is neat and disciplined, the meaning and resonance lingering and deep—resounding like the music of a flourishing age, it can tower over all the other compositions.
Examiner, County Director of Studies Cheng, comments: The framework is upright and grand; the moral principles are precise and thorough.
Examiner, County Director of Studies Zhou, comments: Clear and vigorous, worthy of recitation.

Observe how the dukes and ministers exhaust their reverence in the sacrifice, and the blessings of the spirits follow upon it. Now, sacrifice takes reverence as its core. When one has exhausted one's reverence, the spirits' bestowal of blessings upon him also corresponds in each case to its kind. The singer of the "Chu ci" (Thorny Caltrop) meant to say that sacrifices in the ancestral temple are not performed in order to seek blessings; yet if one sacrifices and does not…

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
受福是神弗享而吾之孝誠未孚矣我公卿而
有是哉彼禮行之久則力竭而易愆也今則自
求神以至于獻尸時雖久而致愨之忱益虔力
已竭而不匱之思罔懈蓋備之爲禮物著之爲
禮容舉莫或愆焉誠盡其敬而敬者由是祝傳
神意以賚孝孫也何如哉蓋曰祭有飲食而芳
潔其至也玆而苾苾芬芬旣莫非神之所嗜矣
則卜爾百福其取諸飲食焉來如幾也多如式
也庶徵與庶羞其相應也已何也敬昭於物而
===
百福之卜也以其敬也非以物也祭有禮容而
莊敬其至也玆而齊稷匡敕旣莫非神之所歆
矣則永錫爾極其取諸禮容焉時萬善也時億
善也多福與多儀其相應也已何也敬見於容
而爾極之錫也以其敬也非以容也此其式禮
謹而孝誠備類應速而顯道彰公卿盡祭之義
如此非德盛政脩何以致之抑不求其爲孝子
之祭也而嘏詞以類應賚之何哉蓋不期福者
固奉祭之心而祀典之舉肇于力農則宜稼于
punctuated: 受福，是神弗享，而吾之孝誠未孚矣。我公卿而有是哉？彼禮行之久，則力竭而易愆也；今則自求神以至于獻尸，時雖久而致愨之忱益虔，力已竭而不匱之思罔懈。蓋備之爲禮物，著之爲禮容，舉莫或愆焉，誠盡其敬而敬者。由是祝傳神意以賚孝孫也，何如哉？蓋曰：祭有飲食，而芳潔其至也。玆而苾苾芬芬，旣莫非神之所嗜矣，則卜爾百福，其取諸飲食焉，來如幾也，多如式也，庶徵與庶羞其相應也已。何也？敬昭於物，而百福之卜也，以其敬也，非以物也。祭有禮容，而莊敬其至也。玆而齊稷匡敕，旣莫非神之所歆矣，則永錫爾極，其取諸禮容焉，時萬善也，時億善也，多福與多儀其相應也已。何也？敬見於容，而爾極之錫也，以其敬也，非以容也。此其式禮謹而孝誠備，類應速而顯道彰，公卿盡祭之義如此，非德盛政脩，何以致之？抑不求其爲孝子之祭也，而嘏詞以類應賚之，何哉？蓋不期福者，固奉祭之心；而祀典之舉，肇于力農，則宜稼于…
translation_en: …receive blessings, this would mean the spirits do not accept the offering and our filial sincerity has not inspired trust. Could such a thing happen with our dukes and ministers? When ritual proceedings are protracted, one's strength is exhausted and it is easy to commit faults. Yet now, from invoking the spirits to presenting offerings to the impersonator of the dead, although the time is long, the sincerity of their utmost devotion grows ever more reverent; although their strength is exhausted, their unfailing thoughts of filial piety never slacken. Indeed, whether prepared as ritual offerings or manifested as ritual demeanor, in nothing do they err; they truly fulfill their reverence and remain reverent. Thereupon, how is it when the invocators convey the will of the spirits to bestow blessings upon the filial descendant? It may be said: sacrifices involve food and drink, in which fragrance and purity are paramount. Now that these offerings are so sweet and fragrant, there is nothing the spirits do not relish; thus, they "grant you a hundred blessings," drawing the analogy from the food and drink—coming at the due time and in the proper abundance, the manifold auspicious responses corresponding to the manifold delicacies. Why is this? Because reverence is made manifest in the offerings, and the granting of a hundred blessings is due to that reverence, not to the material offerings themselves. Sacrifices also involve ritual demeanor, in which solemnity and reverence are paramount. Now that they are so composed, swift, upright, and cautious, there is nothing the spirits do not delight in; thus, they "forever bestow upon you the utmost good," drawing the analogy from the ritual demeanor—bringing ten thousand blessings and a hundred million blessings, the abundance of fortune corresponding to the abundance of ceremony. Why is this? Because reverence is revealed in the demeanor, and the bestowal of the utmost good is due to that reverence, not to the outward demeanor itself. Herein, their observance of ritual is scrupulous and their filial sincerity complete; the response in kind is swift and the manifest Way is illuminated. That the dukes and ministers fulfill the meaning of sacrifice in such a manner—without flourishing virtue and well-ordered governance, how could they achieve this? Yet a filial son's sacrifice does not seek reward; why then do the words of blessing reward him with responses in kind? Indeed, not expecting blessings is naturally the mind of one who performs a sacrifice. However, the institution of sacrificial rites begins with diligent husbandry; thus, making the grain thrive in…

千畝而匱神之祀者視此爲何如
敬之敬之天惟顯思命不易哉
陶志高

周臣亟勉君以敬而指天命以示警焉夫敬者
祈天永命之本也以此告其君而忠愛之情見
乎詞矣宜成王述之以自警也其言曰天之立
君豈其使一人晏然於民上已哉固有所保
天命者在也臣之願王何如其必履崇高之勢
毋徒優游焉也而圖惟於密勿者恒切時幾之
敕撫盈成之運毋徒逸豫焉也而主宰於淵衷
punctuated:
田，順氣成象，明德已先黍稷而馨矣。故孔子曰：「我祭則必受福。」其克享也又何疑？噫！后之不藉千畝而匱神之祀者，視此爲何如？

「敬之敬之，天惟顯思，命不易哉。」
陶志高
同考試官教諭陳批：格調平正，詞致宏朗，發天命處尤透。
同考試官教諭陳批：意足格高，不落時套，惟見此篇。
考試官教諭程批：詞簡意明，文之復古者。
考試官教諭周批：冲雅。

周臣亟勉君以敬，而指天命以示警焉。夫敬者，祈天永命之本也。以此告其君，而忠愛之情見乎詞矣。宜成王述之以自警也！其言曰：天之立君，豈其使一人晏然於民上已哉？固有所保天命者在也。臣之願王何如？其必履崇高之勢，毋徒優游焉也，而圖惟於密勿者，恒切時幾之敕；撫盈成之運，毋徒逸豫焉也，而主宰於淵衷…
translation_en:
…the fields, harmonious vital energy forms its manifestations, and luminous virtue has already sent forth its fragrance even before the millet is offered. Therefore Confucius said, "Whenever I sacrifice, I am sure to receive blessings." What doubt, then, can there be that the spirits accept the offering? Alas! How do later rulers, who fail to plow the thousand-mu sacred field and thereby impoverish the sacrifices to the spirits, compare with this?

"Be reverent, be reverent! Heaven is splendidly manifest; its Mandate is not easily preserved."
Tao Zhigao 陶志高
Associate Examiner Instructor Chen comments: The style and tone are balanced and upright, the diction and expression grand and clear; where it expounds upon the Mandate of Heaven, it is especially penetrating.
Associate Examiner Instructor Chen comments: The meaning is ample and the style lofty, not falling into contemporary clichés—seen only in this essay.
Examiner Instructor Cheng comments: Concise in wording and clear in meaning, a piece that returns to antiquity in style.
Examiner Instructor Zhou comments: Serene and elegant.

The Zhou ministers earnestly urged their sovereign to be reverent, pointing to the Mandate of Heaven to serve as a warning. Now, reverence is the foundation for praying to Heaven for an enduring Mandate. When they spoke thus to their sovereign, their feelings of loyalty and devotion were manifest in their words. Fitting indeed was it that King Cheng recounted them in order to admonish himself! Their words were to this effect: When Heaven establishes a ruler, could it merely be to let one man sit in comfort and ease above the people? Assuredly, there is that by which the Mandate of Heaven is preserved. What, then, do your servants wish for Your Majesty? Occupying the position of supreme eminence, may you not merely indulge in leisurely ease, but in planning with diligent care in secret, ever feel an urgent charge to attend to the timely springs of action; presiding over an era of abundance and accomplishment, may you not merely give yourself over to idle pleasure, but in governing the depths of your heart…

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
者常存嚴翼之思尚其敬之哉敬之哉而何言
乎其當敬也蓋人君所事者惟天而其所以得
爲天子者惟其受天之命也今以言乎天命則
冲漠無朕之中而監觀爲之有赫其克敬也天
必知之而命之留者恒因之其所以使命之必
我留者不易也太虛無物之表而臨下爲之孔
昭其弗敬也天必知之而命之去者恒因之其
所以使命之不我去者不易也知天之惟顯則
當思所以格天知命之不易則當思所以保命
===
卽日兢業以圖之猶懼天之難忱而命之不常
也尚可以不敬哉吁周臣以此告成王而王且
述之則所以祈天永命者必有道矣抑是道也
固心法也亦周之家法也文之敬止武之敬勝
謨烈昭然在也何他求乎卒之成王能緝熙光
明而夙夜敬止凡以畏天之威而繼序不忘也
其用諸臣之言而以法祖爲事者乎是故思敬
天者惟在於法祖
春秋
punctuated:
者，常存嚴翼之思，尚其敬之哉！敬之哉！而何言乎其當敬也？蓋人君所事者惟天，而其所以得爲天子者，惟其受天之命也。今以言乎天命，則冲漠無朕之中，而監觀爲之有赫。其克敬也，天必知之，而命之留者恒因之；其所以使命之必我留者，不易也。太虛無物之表，而臨下爲之孔昭。其弗敬也，天必知之，而命之去者恒因之；其所以使命之不我去者，不易也。知天之惟顯，則當思所以格天；知命之不易，則當思所以保命。即日兢業以圖之，猶懼天之難忱，而命之不常也，尚可以不敬哉！吁！周臣以此告成王，而王且述之，則所以祈天永命者，必有道矣。抑是道也，固心法也，亦周之家法也。文之敬止，武之敬勝，謨烈昭然在也，何他求乎？卒之成王能緝熙光明，而夙夜敬止，凡以畏天之威，而繼序不忘也。其用諸臣之言，而以法祖爲事者乎！是故思敬天者，惟在於法祖。

春秋
translation_en:
… constantly maintains thoughts of solemn reverence—may he indeed be reverent!“

”Be reverent!“ Why does one say that he ought to be reverent? It is because what a ruler serves is Heaven alone, and the reason he is able to be the Son of Heaven is solely that he has received the Mandate of Heaven. Now, to speak of the Mandate of Heaven: within the vast emptiness without a sign, its watchful gaze is awesomely bright. When one is able to be reverent, Heaven surely knows it, and the Mandate's remaining always follows from this; yet causing the Mandate certainly to remain with us is not easy. Beyond the great void where nothing exists, its supervision over the world below is utterly clear. When one is not reverent, Heaven surely knows it, and the Mandate's departure always follows from this; thus causing the Mandate not to depart from us is not easy. Knowing that Heaven is so manifest, one must think of how to reach Heaven; knowing that the Mandate is not easy to keep, one must think of how to preserve the Mandate. Even if one strives for it day by day with cautious diligence, one still fears that Heaven is hard to rely upon and that the Mandate is inconstant—how could one dare not be reverent!

Alas! The ministers of Zhou admonished King Cheng with these words, and the King moreover recounted them; thus there must have been a Way by which he prayed to Heaven for an enduring Mandate. Furthermore, this Way is indeed the method of the mind, and it is also the family law of the House of Zhou. King Wen's resting in reverence and King Wu's triumph through reverence—their counsels and meritorious deeds are brightly present; why seek elsewhere? In the end, King Cheng was able to continue the bright illumination and be reverent morning and night, all because he stood in awe of the majesty of Heaven and did not forget to carry on the succession. Did he not employ the words of his ministers and make emulating his ancestors his occupation? Therefore, for one who wishes to revere Heaven, it lies solely in emulating one's ancestors.

Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
楚人侵鄭〔僖公二年〕齊人執陳轅濤塗〔僖公四年〕
方學龍
同考試官訓導趙批詞平平爾而曲折開闔
處卓有先輩矩矱豈以格勝者乎取之
考試官敎諭程批格嚴語練
考試官敎諭周批明整
伯德之動怠於人心之思斁驗之矣此鄭被兵
而興思陳同好而見斁皆由於桓德之所召也
===
嘗謂王伯之辨惟德之誠偽爾王者感人惟誠
故人心思之愈久不忘伯者異是有思未幾而
厭卽至矣何不引齊桓之事明之夫鄭之見侵
於楚也以卽夏也於時聃伯被囚鄭患蓋孔棘
矣使桓無德以聯其志則鋌而走險奚擇焉惟
自會檉以來念深禮謹志切安攘彼鄭亦已諒
之故三揖可擣五廟可震寧以國斃而不肯納
款於南荆也觀孔叔之言曰齊方勤我棄德不
祥吁名其爲德且完守以待之思可知也古有
punctuated:
楚人侵鄭〔僖公二年〕，齊人執陳轅濤塗〔僖公四年〕。
方學龍
同考試官訓導趙批：詞平平爾，而曲折開闔處卓有先輩矩矱，豈以格勝者乎？取之。
考試官敎諭程批：格嚴語練。
考試官敎諭周批：明整。
伯德之動怠，於人心之思斁驗之矣。此鄭被兵而興思，陳同好而見斁，皆由於桓德之所召也。嘗謂王伯之辨，惟德之誠偽爾。王者感人惟誠，故人心思之，愈久不忘；伯者異是，有思未幾而厭卽至矣。何不引齊桓之事明之？夫鄭之見侵於楚也，以卽夏也。於時聃伯被囚，鄭患蓋孔棘矣。使桓無德以聯其志，則鋌而走險，奚擇焉？惟自會檉以來，念深禮謹，志切安攘，彼鄭亦已諒之。故三揖可擣，五廟可震，寧以國斃而不肯納款於南荆也。觀孔叔之言曰：「齊方勤我，棄德不祥。」吁！名其爲德，且完守以待之，思可知也。古有
translation_en:
"The men of Chu invaded Zheng" [Second Year of Duke Xi]; "The men of Qi seized Yuan Taotu of Chen" [Fourth Year of Duke Xi].

Fang Xuelong 方學龍

Associate Examiner, Assistant Instructor Zhao 趙 comments: The phrasing is unpretentious, yet in its turns and structural openings and closings it outstandingly possesses the standards and models of the predecessors. Is it not one that triumphs through structural form? Selected.
Examiner, Instructor Cheng 程 comments: The structure is rigorous and the diction is polished.
Examiner, Instructor Zhou 周 comments: Clear and well-ordered.

The diligence and laxity of a hegemon's virtue can be verified by the longing or weariness in men's hearts. Thus, that Zheng suffered armed attack and yet conceived a longing for him, whereas Chen shared in amity and yet grew weary of him, were both brought about by the state of Duke Huan's 桓公 virtue.

It has been said that the distinction between a true king and a hegemon lies solely in the sincerity or falsity of their virtue. A true king moves men by sincerity alone, and therefore men's hearts long for him, never forgetting him the longer time passes. A hegemon is different from this: men may long for him, yet before much time has passed, weariness immediately arrives. Why not cite the affairs of Duke Huan of Qi 齊桓公 to make this clear?

Now, Zheng's being invaded by Chu 楚 was because it had aligned itself with the central Xia 夏 states. At that time, Danbo 聃伯 was taken prisoner, and Zheng's crisis was indeed extremely urgent. Had Duke Huan lacked the virtue to bind their resolve, then in desperation they would have taken any reckless risk—what choice would they have made? Only because ever since the meeting at Cheng 檉, his concern had been deep and his propriety careful, and his ambition earnestly set on pacifying the interior and repelling the exterior, Zheng for its part already understood and trusted him. Therefore, though their court of three salutations might be struck down and their five ancestral temples shaken, they would rather perish as a state than be willing to offer submission to southern Jing 荆 [Chu]. Looking at the words of Kong Shu 孔叔: "Qi is just now laboring on our behalf; to abandon virtue is inauspicious." Ah! In naming what he did "virtue," and moreover keeping their defenses intact in order to await him, their longing can be known. In antiquity there was…

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
□□斧之勛而致思皇四國者桓其庶幾矣乎
陳大夫之見執於齊也以誤師也當時盟楚而
歸陳適當孔道矣使桓無闕以攜其心則敬共
往來曷二焉惟自服楚以後志驕氣溢漸異曩
時彼陳巳竊異之故慮其誅求懼其撫掠寧以
見討而直欲避兵於東夷也觀轅濤塗之言曰
師出陳鄭國必甚病吁策其必病且設謀以誤
之斁可知也古有抱隕淵之懼而永撫有萬方
者桓其少愧矣乎夫以德之勤即反覆如鄭可
===
使委心於我繼之以怠宇下之陳不免斁心焉
甚矣感人當以誠也此王伯之分也說者謂鄭
之勤也親暱罔棄也仲之教也執陳之日仲不
在側耶無亦積慮以圖所志惟一楚乎楚服而
君主德色寖不如昔有以也噫此伯者所以爲
假而管仲君子不爲與
春白狄來襄公十有八年
施夢麟
同考試官訓導趙 批 是作場中知體傳意者少
punctuated:
□□斧之勛，而致思皇四國者，桓其庶幾矣乎！陳大夫之見執於齊也，以誤師也。當時盟楚而歸，陳適當孔道矣。使桓無闕以攜其心，則敬共往來，曷二焉？惟自服楚以後，志驕氣溢，漸異曩時，彼陳巳竊異之。故慮其誅求，懼其撫掠，寧以見討，而直欲避兵於東夷也。觀轅濤塗之言曰：「師出陳鄭，國必甚病。」吁！策其必病，且設謀以誤之，斁可知也。古有抱隕淵之懼，而永撫有萬方者，桓其少愧矣乎！夫以德之勤，即反覆如鄭，可使委心於我；繼之以怠，宇下之陳，不免斁心焉。甚矣，感人當以誠也！此王伯之分也。說者謂鄭之勤也，親暱罔棄也，仲之教也。執陳之日，仲不在側耶？無亦積慮以圖所志，惟一楚乎？楚服而君主德色，寖不如昔，有以也。噫！此伯者所以爲假，而管仲君子不爲與！

《春，白狄來（襄公十有八年）》
施夢麟
同考試官訓導趙批：是作場中知體傳意者少，
translation_en:
… [achieved] the merit of the broken battle-axes [of the Duke of Zhou] and caused the four quarters of the realm to long for him in admiration—Duke Huan came quite close to this, did he not?

As for the grandee of Chen being seized by Qi, it was because he misdirected the army. At that time, returning after concluding the covenant with Chu, Chen happened to lie right along the main thoroughfare. Had Duke Huan been free of faults that alienated their hearts, they would have reverently attended to the traffic back and forth—how could there have been any duplicity? Only, ever since he subjugated Chu, his ambition grew arrogant and his spirit overflowed, gradually differing from earlier days, and Chen had already secretly noted the change. Therefore, worrying about his exactions and fearing his plundering [?], they would rather face punitive attack and simply sought to divert the troops toward the Eastern Yi. Look at the words of Yuan Taotu, who said: "If the army marches out through Chen and Zheng, our states will certainly suffer grievously." Alas! Calculating that they would certainly suffer, and moreover devising a scheme to misdirect them, their weariness of him can be known. In antiquity there was one who held the fear of falling into an abyss and forever cherished and possessed the myriad regions—must not Duke Huan feel somewhat ashamed before him?

Now, through diligence in virtue, even a vacillating state like Zheng could be made to entrust its heart to us; yet when followed by negligence, even Chen under our very shelter could not avoid growing weary at heart. How true it is that moving others must be done with sincerity! This is the distinction between the true king and the hegemon. Commentators say that the diligence shown toward Zheng—not abandoning those who are close and intimate—was the teaching of Guan Zhong. On the day Chen's minister was seized, was Zhong not by his side? Or was it not rather that all their accumulated deliberations in pursuit of their ambition were fixed solely upon Chu? Once Chu submitted, both lord and minister put on airs of self-satisfaction and gradually ceased to be as they were in the past—there was a reason for it. Alas! Is this not why the hegemon is merely a counterfeit, and why a gentleman refuses to be a Guan Zhong?

"In spring, the White Di came." (Eighteenth year of Duke Xiang)
Shi Menglin

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
子獨探其大旨而詞復偉雋是苦心者錄之
考試官教諭程批〔得聖人意〕
考試官教諭周批〔詞旨明確〕
春秋於外夷交內而深示謹防之意焉蓋防正
而后淫慝之患可弭也經於白狄之來所為深
致意與昔白狄世處陰山與曲阜不通舊矣一
旦藩飾而來倘亦徼福於周公以踵越裳之遺
意乎君子則曰狄非可朝於魯也而魯何為受
之蓋中國與夷狄畫疆而居無時可通者故以
===
天子之尊且世僅一見焉以元聖之德且不享
其物焉其所以正防而禁慝固甚嚴也魯也龜
蒙之封無改於舊成襄以來代有失德何政而
格於狄今之來也果款我乎抑嘗我乎未可知
也馳一介而拒之國門斯非魯之所得為者哉
顧乃位非天子而徒慕柔遠之名德非聖人而
妄徼執贄之獻其亦不自量也已想其受玉於
庭薦器於廟魯之君臣色動亦以為一時盛美
矣獨不思無故而涉吾之境其漸不可長也非
punctuated:
子獨探其大旨，而詞復偉雋，是苦心者，錄之。
考試官教諭程批：〔得聖人意。〕
考試官教諭周批：〔詞旨明確。〕
《春秋》於外夷交內，而深示謹防之意焉。蓋防正而后淫慝之患可弭也，經於白狄之來，所為深致意與！昔白狄世處陰山，與曲阜不通舊矣。一旦藩飾而來，倘亦徼福於周公，以踵越裳之遺意乎？君子則曰：「狄非可朝於魯也，而魯何為受之？」蓋中國與夷狄畫疆而居，無時可通者。故以天子之尊，且世僅一見焉；以元聖之德，且不享其物焉。其所以正防而禁慝，固甚嚴也。魯也，龜、蒙之封無改於舊，成、襄以來，代有失德，何政而格於狄？今之來也，果款我乎？抑嘗我乎？未可知也。馳一介而拒之國門，斯非魯之所得為者哉！顧乃位非天子，而徒慕柔遠之名；德非聖人，而妄徼執贄之獻，其亦不自量也已！想其受玉於庭，薦器於廟，魯之君臣色動，亦以為一時盛美矣。獨不思無故而涉吾之境，其漸不可長也；非
translation_en:
… you alone grasped its central import, and your phrasing is moreover grand and incisive. This is the work of one who has taken great pains; let it be selected for publication.

Examiner, Instructor Cheng, comments: 〔He has grasped the sage's intent.〕
Examiner, Instructor Zhou, comments: 〔The phrasing and purport are clear and precise.〕

When foreign tribes had dealings with the interior, the Spring and Autumn Annals deeply expressed the principle of maintaining strict defenses. For only when the defenses are rectified can the perils of licentiousness and evil be forestalled; is this not why the Classic paid such deep attention to the coming of the Baidi? In antiquity, the Baidi dwelt for generations in the Yin Mountains and for long had no communication with Qufu. When one day they came in ceremonial array as vassals, could it be that they too sought blessings from the Duke of Zhou, following in the footsteps of the legacy of Yuechang? Yet the gentleman says: "The Di are not such as may pay court to Lu; why then did Lu receive them?" For the Central States and the foreign tribes live within demarcated boundaries and should at no time have direct intercourse. Thus, even with the exalted status of the Son of Heaven, they were granted audience only once in a generation; even with the virtue of the Great Sage, their tribute goods were not enjoyed. The means by which defenses were rectified and evil prohibited were strict indeed. As for Lu, its fief of Mounts Gui and Meng was unchanged from of old, yet since the reigns of Dukes Cheng and Xiang, generation after generation had been wanting in virtue—what governance did it possess that could reach and move the Di? In coming now, were they truly offering us sincere allegiance, or were they testing us? That could not be known. To dispatch a single messenger and refuse them at the gates of the capital—was this not what Lu ought to have done? Instead, though not holding the position of the Son of Heaven, Lu vainly coveted the reputation of cherishing those from afar; though not possessing the virtue of a sage, it presumptuously sought the presentation of ceremonial gifts. How utterly it failed to take its own measure! One can imagine that when receiving the jade in the courtyard and presenting the vessels in the ancestral temple, the ruler and ministers of Lu were visibly moved, regarding it as a splendid triumph of the age. Only they failed to reflect that for foreigners to cross our borders without cause is a tendency that must not be allowed to grow; and where…

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
所及而妄受人之朝其禮不可行也率是爲之
是使異類得接軫於神明之區內外之防紊矣
狡焉得肆乎窺伺之計淫慝之禍滋矣世道之
亂也其何日之有故春秋直書白狄曰來而不
與其朝所以一內外懲淫慝也而譏魯之意至
深切矣惟此義不明然后有與夷狄交婚居羌
胡內塞蓋至於中原多事神州陸沉而后知聖
人謹白狄之意深也彼有閉關謝西域者其庶
幾得春秋之旨
===
禮記
是故樂之隆非極音也食饗之禮非致味
也清廟之瑟朱絃而疏越壹倡而三歎
有遺音者矣大饗之禮尚玄酒而俎腥
魚大羹不和有遺味者矣
李繼韶
同考試官訓導王批體認親切而鎔詞布調
咸歸大雅子殆深於禮樂者
考試官教諭程批和平之音
punctuated:
所及而妄受人之朝，其禮不可行也。率是爲之，是使異類得接軫於神明之區，內外之防紊矣；狡焉得肆乎窺伺之計，淫慝之禍滋矣。世道之亂也，其何日之有？故《春秋》直書白狄曰「來」，而不與其朝，所以一內外、懲淫慝也，而譏魯之意至深切矣。惟此義不明，然后有與夷狄交婚、居羌胡內塞，蓋至於中原多事、神州陸沉，而后知聖人謹白狄之意深也。彼有閉關謝西域者，其庶幾得《春秋》之旨。

《禮記》
「是故樂之隆，非極音也；食饗之禮，非致味也。清廟之瑟，朱絃而疏越，壹倡而三歎，有遺音者矣。大饗之禮，尚玄酒而俎腥魚，大羹不和，有遺味者矣。」
李繼韶
同考試官訓導王批：體認親切，而鎔詞布調，咸歸大雅，子殆深於禮樂者。
考試官教諭程批：和平之音。
translation_en:
…within their proper reach, and recklessly accepting homage at court from others is a ritual that cannot be practiced. To act in accordance with this is to allow alien peoples to link their carriage-wheels in the realm of the sacred and enlightened, throwing the boundary between inner and outer into confusion; the crafty are thus able to indulge their schemes of spying and probing, and the disasters of licentiousness and evil proliferate. How many days would it take for the moral order of the world to fall into chaos? Therefore, the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) directly records of the Baidi simply that they "came," refusing to grant them the term "court audience," in order to unify the distinction between inner and outer and to chastise licentiousness and evil—and its intent in criticizing Lu is profound and trenchant indeed. Only when this principle was obscured did there later come to be intermarriage with the Yi and Di barbarians and the settlement of Qiang and Hu tribes within the frontier passes; only when the Central Plains were beset by troubles and the Sacred Land sank into ruin did people finally realize how profound was the Sage's intent in guarding against the Baidi. As for that ruler who closed the frontier passes and declined relations with the Western Regions, he came close to grasping the purport of the Spring and Autumn Annals.

Record of Rites (Liji)
"Therefore, the height of music does not lie in the utmost elaboration of sound; the rites of banquets and feasts do not lie in the perfection of flavors. The zither of the Pure Temple has vermilion strings and widely spaced sound-holes; when one leads the singing and three join in sighing response, there is a lingering sound left unexpressed. In the rites of the Great Feast, plain water takes precedence, raw fish is placed on the offering stand, and the great broth is unseasoned; there is a lingering flavor left unexpressed."
Li Jishao 
Associate Examiner Assistant Instructor Wang comments: His personal comprehension is intimate and exact, while his casting of phrases and arrangement of cadence all return to refined elegance; you are surely one deeply versed in ritual and music.
Examiner Instructor Cheng comments: Tones of harmony and peace.

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
考試官教諭周批旨趣雋永
論禮樂不尚乎文即其至者而可知也夫音與
味皆禮樂之文而非其至也試觀清廟大饗蓋
可覩已樂記意曰禮樂之道有本而立有藉而
行彼以音求樂以味求禮者非善論禮樂者也
何則音以宣樂人皆曰樂之隆隆于音之極矣
不知至樂無聲有播于音而不盡於音者在何
極音之足云也味以成禮人皆曰禮之盛盛于
味之致矣不知至敬無文有寓于味而不專于
===
味者存何致味之足云也曷以徵之彼清廟之
瑟非樂之隆者乎語其音則為朱絃為疏越壹
倡三歎而已吾未聞其音之極也然音雖淡也
而移風易俗之機蘊焉徐而聽之蓋宛然見聖
人於心而有遺音矣孰謂樂之隆也而極音乎
哉大饗之禮非禮之盛者乎語其味則為玄酒
為腥魚大羹不和而已吾未見其味之致也然
味雖淡也而報本反始之情著焉徐而玩之蓋
儼然見祖考于心而有遺味矣孰謂禮之盛也
punctuated:
考試官教諭周批：旨趣雋永。

論禮樂不尚乎文，即其至者而可知也。夫音與味，皆禮樂之文，而非其至也。試觀清廟、大饗，蓋可覩已。《樂記》意曰：禮樂之道，有本而立，有藉而行。彼以音求樂，以味求禮者，非善論禮樂者也。何則？音以宣樂，人皆曰樂之隆，隆于音之極矣。不知至樂無聲，有播于音而不盡於音者在，何極音之足云也？味以成禮，人皆曰禮之盛，盛于味之致矣。不知至敬無文，有寓于味而不專于味者存，何致味之足云也？曷以徵之？彼清廟之瑟，非樂之隆者乎？語其音，則為朱絃，為疏越，壹倡三歎而已，吾未聞其音之極也。然音雖淡也，而移風易俗之機蘊焉。徐而聽之，蓋宛然見聖人於心，而有遺音矣。孰謂樂之隆也，而極音乎哉？大饗之禮，非禮之盛者乎？語其味，則為玄酒，為腥魚，大羹不和而已，吾未見其味之致也。然味雖淡也，而報本反始之情著焉。徐而玩之，蓋儼然見祖考于心，而有遺味矣。孰謂禮之盛也，
translation_en:
Comment by Examiner and Instructor Zhou: Its import and charm are enduring and profound.

Discussing how ritual and music do not prize outward ornament, one can know this simply by looking at their highest expressions. Now, musical tones and culinary flavors are both the outward ornaments of ritual and music, and not their highest essence. If one examines the music of the "Pure Temple" (Qingmiao) and the ritual of the Great Sacrificial Feast (daxiang), this can indeed be seen.

The meaning of the Record of Music (Yueji) is to say: The Way of ritual and music is established upon a fundamental root and practiced by relying on outward forms. Those who seek music merely through tones and seek ritual merely through flavors are not skilled at discussing ritual and music. Why is this? Tones are used to express music, so people all say that the height of music lies in the utmost perfection of its tones. They do not know that supreme music is soundless; there is something that is conveyed through tones yet is not exhausted by tones—how could the utmost perfection of tones be worth speaking of? Flavors are used to complete ritual, so people all say that the flourishing of ritual lies in the utmost refinement of its flavors. They do not know that supreme reverence is unadorned; there is something that lodges in flavors yet does not reside exclusively in flavors—how could the utmost refinement of flavors be worth speaking of?

How can this be verified? Is not the zither of the "Pure Temple" the height of music? Speaking of its tones, there are only vermilion strings, widely spaced sound-holes, and one lead voice with three voices sighing in response—I have not heard of its tones being carried to the extreme. Yet although the tones are bland, the subtle mechanism for transforming customs and changing habits is contained therein. Listening to it unhurriedly, one seems to vividly behold the sages in one's heart, and there is a lingering sound beyond the notes. Who would say that the height of music consists in carrying tones to the extreme? Is not the ritual of the Great Sacrificial Feast the flourishing of ritual? Speaking of its flavors, there are only dark酒 [water offered as wine], raw fish on the sacrificial stand, and the great meat broth unseasoned—I have not seen its flavors being carried to the utmost refinement. Yet although the flavors are bland, the sentiment of repaying one's roots and returning to the beginning is manifested therein. Savoring it unhurriedly, one seems to solemnly behold the ancestral forefathers in one's heart, and there is a lingering flavor beyond the taste. Who would say that the flourishing of ritual…

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
而致味乎哉是蓋求禮樂于音味之内其機也
淺禮樂皆虛也求禮樂于音味之外其蓄也深
禮樂皆實也君子察此可以明禮樂矣抑考諸
易曰殷薦上帝傳曰告民力之普存則音與味
顧可少與吁記者特爲狥末忘本者戒耳後世
不探其本而徒於鐘鼓籩豆之間求之抑末矣
其如禮樂何哉是故禮樂之興蓋必有中正和
平之蘊者而後可
子云善則稱君過則稱己則民作忠君陳
===
曰爾有嘉謀嘉猷入告爾君于内女乃
順之于外曰此謀此猷惟我君之德於
乎是惟良顯哉
陳治則
同考試官訓導王批 人臣忠君之義闡明殆
盡而一結尤見忠悃
考試官教諭程批 平淡中有逸趣
考試官教諭周批 蘊蓄醇雅
人臣忠君之化觀諸書而可證也夫事君以忠
punctuated:
而致味乎哉？是蓋求禮樂于音味之内，其機也淺，禮樂皆虛也；求禮樂于音味之外，其蓄也深，禮樂皆實也。君子察此，可以明禮樂矣。抑考諸《易》曰：「殷薦上帝。」《傳》曰：「告民力之普存。」則音與味顧可少與？吁！記者特爲狥末忘本者戒耳。後世不探其本，而徒於鐘鼓籩豆之間求之，抑末矣，其如禮樂何哉？是故禮樂之興，蓋必有中正和平之蘊者而後可。

子云：「善則稱君，過則稱己，則民作忠。《君陳》曰：『爾有嘉謀嘉猷，入告爾君于内，女乃順之于外，曰：「此謀此猷，惟我君之德。」於乎！是惟良顯哉！』」
陳治則
同考試官訓導王批：人臣忠君之義，闡明殆盡，而一結尤見忠悃。
考試官教諭程批：平淡中有逸趣。
考試官教諭周批：蘊蓄醇雅。

人臣忠君之化，觀諸《書》而可證也。夫事君以忠，
translation_en:
… that it carries flavor to the utmost? For if one seeks ritual and music merely within sound and flavor, their inner workings are shallow, and ritual and music are both hollow; if one seeks ritual and music beyond sound and flavor, what they store up is deep, and ritual and music are both substantial. When the gentleman examines this, he can understand ritual and music. Yet if we consult the Book of Changes (Yi), which says, "offering grandly to the Lord on High," and the Zuo Commentary (Zhuan), which says, "announcing that the people's strength is universally preserved," then how could sound and flavor actually be dispensed with? Alas! The compiler of the Record was simply giving a warning to those who pursue the branches and forget the root. When later generations fail to explore the root and merely seek it among bells and drums, bamboo and wooden vessels, that is pursuing the branches indeed—what can they do for ritual and music? Therefore, for ritual and music to flourish, there must first be an inner store of impartiality, correctness, harmony, and peace.

The Master said: "When there is goodness, attribute it to the ruler; when there is fault, attribute it to oneself—then the people will be moved to loyalty. The 'Jun Chen' says: 'When you have fine plans and fine counsels, go in and report them to your ruler within; then comply with them outside, saying: "This plan, this counsel, is wholly due to our ruler's virtue." Oh! How good and illustrious this is!'"
Chen Zhize
Comment by Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor Wang: The principle of a minister's loyalty to his ruler is expounded almost exhaustively, and the conclusion especially reveals loyal sincerity.
Comment by Examiner and Instructor Cheng: Within its plainness there is an transcendent charm.
Comment by Examiner and Instructor Zhou: Deeply stored up, pure and refined.

The transforming influence of a minister's loyalty to his ruler can be verified by examining the Book of Documents (Shu). Now, serving one's ruler with loyalty …

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
臣道也而民皆化之可謂良顯矣雖書詞所稱
奚加焉夫子之意謂夫人臣一身君之輔民之
表也惟不能效忠於君斯不能作忠于民難以
語良顯矣誠知善本人所樂道而况臣之於君
有頌德之義焉故無論君之盛德不敢竊爲已
功即善之在我亦舉而讓諸君焉若曰主上聖
明臣子何庸也過本不當自文而况臣之於君
有引慝之分焉故無論吾之失德不敢曲爲掩
護即過之在君亦舉而任諸已焉若曰臣職曠
===
===
違天王何愆也如是則於其稱君也可以觀忠
愛焉而民之遵化者咸起夫頌德之忱於其稱
已也可以觀忠謹焉而民之仰承者咸萌夫引
慝之志始焉以一人之忠作萬民之忠既焉合
萬民之忠皆一人之忠若而臣也誠哉其良顯
矣君陳有云嘉謀嘉猷入而告之于內此謀此
猷出而順之于外而以良顯稱焉吾謂在君陳
以忠于爾后者而垂于紀載固示天下以人臣
之極在君子以忠於吾君者而率乎斯民亦可
punctuated: 臣道也，而民皆化之，可謂良顯矣。雖《書》詞所稱，奚加焉？夫子之意，謂夫人臣一身，君之輔、民之表也。惟不能效忠於君，斯不能作忠于民，難以語良顯矣。誠知善本人所樂道，而况臣之於君，有頌德之義焉。故無論君之盛德不敢竊爲已功，即善之在我，亦舉而讓諸君焉，若曰：「主上聖明，臣子何庸也？」過本不當自文，而况臣之於君，有引慝之分焉。故無論吾之失德不敢曲爲掩護，即過之在君，亦舉而任諸已焉，若曰：「臣職曠違，天王何愆也？」如是，則於其稱君也，可以觀忠愛焉，而民之遵化者，咸起夫頌德之忱；於其稱已也，可以觀忠謹焉，而民之仰承者，咸萌夫引慝之志。始焉以一人之忠，作萬民之忠；既焉合萬民之忠，皆一人之忠。若而臣也，誠哉其良顯矣！《君陳》有云：「嘉謀嘉猷，入而告之于內；此謀此猷，出而順之于外。」而以良顯稱焉。吾謂在君陳，以忠于爾后者而垂于紀載，固示天下以人臣之極；在君子，以忠於吾君者而率乎斯民，亦可
translation_en:
…is the way of a minister, and when the people are all transformed by it, he may be called virtuous and illustrious. Even compared to what is praised in the words of the Book of Documents (Shu), what more could be added?

The Master’s meaning is that a minister, in his own person, is the assistant to the ruler and the exemplar for the people. Only when he fails to devote his loyalty to the ruler is he unable to inspire loyalty in the people, making it difficult to speak of him as virtuous and illustrious.

Suppose he truly understands that goodness is something people naturally delight in speaking of, and how much more so since a minister, in his relation to his ruler, has the duty of praising his virtue. Therefore, not to mention that he would never dare to steal the ruler's abundant virtue as his own merit, even when the goodness lies within himself, he attributes and yields it all to the ruler, as if to say: "The sovereign above is sage and enlightened; what credit belongs to his minister?" And since faults ought never to be glossed over for oneself, how much more so since a minister, in his relation to his ruler, has the obligation of taking blame upon himself. Therefore, not to mention that he would never dare to deviously cover up his own lapses in virtue, even when the fault lies with the ruler, he takes it all upon himself as his own responsibility, as if to say: "In my ministerial office I have been negligent and wayward; what transgression has the Heavenly King committed?"

When he acts like this, then in the way he speaks of his ruler, one can observe his loyal affection, and the people who follow his transforming influence all arouse in themselves a sincere desire to praise their sovereign's virtue; and in the way he speaks of himself, one can observe his loyal circumspection, and the people who look up to and follow him all conceive the resolve to take blame upon themselves. At first, through the loyalty of one man, he stirs up the loyalty of the myriad people; eventually, uniting the loyalty of the myriad people, it all becomes the loyalty of that one man. Such a minister—truly, he is virtuous and illustrious!

In the "Jun Chen" chapter it is said: "Fine plans and fine counsels, he enters and announces them within; these plans and these counsels, he goes forth and complies with them without," and for this he is praised as virtuous and illustrious. I would say that in the case of Jun Chen, by being loyal to his sovereign and having this handed down in the historical records, he certainly showed the empire the ultimate standard of a minister; and in the case of the noble man, by being loyal to our ruler and thereby leading these people, he too may…

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
無愧于良顯之風然則爲臣而不以忠自處者
其亦未玩君陳之義云雖然讓善引過忠矣而
面折廷諍非與蓋都俞喜起上臣之至願也繩
愆糾謬諍臣之不得已也人主諒其不得已之
心而上下其交孚矣是故效忠者臣而作忠者
尤在于君
第貳塲
論
天下國家之大務
葉秉敬
同考試官敎諭陳批天下國家之務有要有本
不博綜玄覽出入古今經世之術異占其槩矣
同考試官敎諭陳批不習竅言直攄要指非明
于當世之務者其何能言錄之以式多士
考試官敎諭程批才情具足機軸圓融
考試官敎諭周批旨明詞達
凡治之難非其治之難也有本之難有要之難
也非有要不足以成天下之務非有本不足以
punctuated:
無愧于良顯之風。然則爲臣而不以忠自處者，其亦未玩《君陳》之義云。雖然，讓善引過，忠矣，而面折廷諍非與？蓋都俞喜起，上臣之至願也；繩愆糾謬，諍臣之不得已也。人主諒其不得已之心，而上下其交孚矣。是故效忠者臣，而作忠者尤在于君。

第貳塲
論
天下國家之大務
葉秉敬
同考試官敎諭陳批：天下國家之務，有要有本。不博綜玄覽，出入古今，經世之術異占其槩矣。
同考試官敎諭陳批：不習竅言，直攄要指，非明于當世之務者，其何能言？錄之以式多士。
考試官敎諭程批：才情具足，機軸圓融。
考試官敎諭周批：旨明詞達。

凡治之難，非其治之難也，有本之難，有要之難也。非有要，不足以成天下之務；非有本，不足以
translation_en:
…have no cause to feel ashamed before the standard of being "good and illustrious." If that is so, then one who serves as a minister without conducting himself in loyalty has surely failed to ponder the meaning of the "Jun Chen" (Book of Documents). Even so, to yield credit for what is good and take blame for faults upon oneself is indeed loyal, yet is not rebuking the ruler to his face and remonstrating at court also loyal? For harmonious agreement and joyful exultation are the highest wish of a superior minister; correcting faults and rectifying errors are what a remonstrating minister does only when he has no choice. When the ruler understands with sympathy this heart that acts out of necessity, then sovereign above and minister below will share mutual trust. Therefore, while it is the minister who renders loyalty, inspiring that loyalty rests above all with the sovereign.

Second Session
Discourse
"The Great Affairs of the Empire and the State"
Ye Bingjing
Associate Examiner and Instructor Chen comments: The affairs of the empire and the state have both essentials and fundamentals. Without broad synthesis and deep contemplation, moving freely between antiquity and the present, how could one grasp the general outline of the art of statecraft [?]?
Associate Examiner and Instructor Chen comments: Not indulging in empty or cliched words [?], he directly sets forth the essential meaning. Were he not someone with a clear understanding of the affairs of the present age, how could he speak thus? We record it to serve as a model for the many scholars.
Examiner and Instructor Cheng comments: Both talent and sensibility are fully present; the structure and pivot of the argument are well-rounded and harmonious.
Examiner and Instructor Zhou comments: The import is clear and the phrasing articulate.

In general, the difficulty of governing does not lie in the governing itself; it lies in the difficulty of grasping the fundamentals and the difficulty of grasping the essentials. Without the essentials, one cannot accomplish the affairs of the empire; without the fundamentals, one cannot…

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
執天下之要何以故也四海之廣兆民之眾延
頸舉踵而待命于一人一人坐視而不為之恤
則恐至于負其望起而徧為之無乃遂至疲神
以為天下勞是故不可以無要操要御詳使天
下不勞而就理非藻飾之所能為也藉第令事
事而廉之而不勝密物物而察之而不勝明是
尚焉能執其要也乎是故不可以無本知本不
匱知要不殆古之人君其于理道亦籌之熟哉
其所以成務未有不繇此者也朱子稱恤民為
===
天下國家之大務而繼之治軍省賦歸之心術
紀綱推本考要有味哉其詳言之也可為世世
法程至明矣嘗試論之天下國家其作室歟要
則樞也本則運是樞以開闔者也其涉川歟要
則舟楫也本則運是舟楫以有濟者也何以明
其然耶聞之曰生民有欲無主乃亂作之君作
之師惟曰其相上帝豈其以一人肆于民上而
淫焉以逞此治之不可以已也而政且鰓鰓然
民且總總然不得其要即欲成務其孰從而成
punctuated: 執天下之要。何以故也？四海之廣，兆民之眾，延頸舉踵而待命于一人。一人坐視而不為之恤，則恐至于負其望；起而徧為之，無乃遂至疲神以為天下勞？是故不可以無要。操要御詳，使天下不勞而就理，非藻飾之所能為也。藉第令事事而廉之，而不勝密；物物而察之，而不勝明。是尚焉能執其要也乎？是故不可以無本。知本不匱，知要不殆。古之人君，其于理道亦籌之熟哉！其所以成務，未有不繇此者也。朱子稱「恤民為天下國家之大務」，而繼之治軍、省賦，歸之心術、紀綱。推本考要，有味哉其詳言之也！可為世世法程，至明矣。嘗試論之：天下國家，其作室歟？要則樞也，本則運是樞以開闔者也。其涉川歟？要則舟楫也，本則運是舟楫以有濟者也。何以明其然耶？聞之曰：「生民有欲，無主乃亂。作之君，作之師，惟曰其相上帝。」豈其以一人肆于民上，而淫焉以逞？此治之不可以已也。而政且鰓鰓然，民且總總然，不得其要，即欲成務，其孰從而成…
translation_en: …grasp the essentials of all under heaven. For what reason is this so? Across the vastness of the Four Seas, the multitudes of millions crane their necks and stand on tiptoe waiting for commands from the One Man. If the One Man sits idle and watches without showing them compassion, there is the fear that he will end up failing their hopes; yet if he rises to attend to every single thing universally, would he not consequently exhaust his spirit and wear himself out for the sake of the empire? For this reason, one cannot do without the essentials. To grasp the essentials in governing the details, so that the empire comes into order without toil, is not something that mere superficial embellishment can achieve. Even supposing one were to investigate every single affair, one could not be thorough enough; if one were to scrutinize every single thing, one could not be discerning enough. How then would one still be able to grasp the essentials? For this reason, one cannot do without the fundamentals. Knowing the fundamentals, one is never depleted; knowing the essentials, one is never imperiled. How thoroughly the rulers of antiquity deliberated upon the way of governance! The means by which they accomplished their affairs never failed to proceed from this. Master Zhu [Zhu Xi 朱熹] declared that "showing compassion for the people is the great affair of the empire and the state," and he followed this with governing the military and reducing taxes, tracing it all back to the ruler's disposition of mind and the guiding threads of statecraft. Probing the fundamentals and examining the essentials—how rich in meaning are his detailed words! That they may serve as a standard and model for generation after generation is utterly clear. Let us attempt to discuss it: Are the empire and the state like building a house? Then the essentials are the door-pivot, and the fundamentals are what turns this pivot so that it opens and closes. Or are they like crossing a river? Then the essentials are the boat and oars, and the fundamentals are what plies this boat and its oars to make the crossing. How can we make it clear that this is so? We have heard it said: "The people are born with desires; without a ruler, they fall into disorder. Heaven made for them a ruler and made for them a teacher, solely that he might assist the Supreme Lord." Could it be that this was done so that one man might act without restraint above the people and indulge himself at will? This is why governance cannot be dispensed with. Yet when administrative affairs are so anxiously complex and the people so numerous and teeming, if one does not grasp the essentials, even if one wishes to accomplish the tasks of state, how could one possibly accomplish…

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
之故驟而語恤民民不可得而恤也驟而言□
賦賦不可得而省也治軍而後省賦可言省賦
而後恤民可舉也故曰要其樞也舟楫也而猶
未也語曰事在四方要在中央聖人執要四方
來效此亦甚未易也君人者誠中心無爲而守
至正其大綱必舉其衆紀必張其軍制必明其
賦斂必省其恩澤必下究否者軍彌治實彌亂
名曰省賦而實繁之民未見德也此夫務華絕
根忘其大者也故曰運樞以開闔運舟楫以有
===
濟則存乎其本也將執天下之要以成天下之
務意在斯乎人君知其然是故廑之乎恤民而
急之乎軍賦重之乎紀綱而根之乎心術心術
正紀綱立吾朝治軍而賦暮省吾暮省賦而民
朝甦不煩指顧不動聲色而天下遂以大治何
以明其然耶昔也時雍于唐風動于虞民何以
至此極也遊堯天戴舜日彼固無用此贅軍冗
賦爲也所無用者獨其軍賦哉兢兢然業業然
根本之地誠先之也後及三代而鋤强取暴軍
punctuated: 之？故驟而語恤民，民不可得而恤也；驟而言□賦，賦不可得而省也。治軍而後省賦可言，省賦而後恤民可舉也。故曰：要，其樞也，舟楫也。而猶未也。語曰：「事在四方，要在中央；聖人執要，四方來效。」此亦甚未易也。君人者誠中心無爲而守至正，其大綱必舉，其衆紀必張，其軍制必明，其賦斂必省，其恩澤必下究。否者，軍彌治，實彌亂，名曰省賦而實繁之，民未見德也。此夫務華絕根，忘其大者也。故曰：運樞以開闔，運舟楫以有濟，則存乎其本也。將執天下之要以成天下之務，意在斯乎？人君知其然，是故廑之乎恤民，而急之乎軍賦，重之乎紀綱，而根之乎心術。心術正，紀綱立，吾朝治軍而賦暮省，吾暮省賦而民朝甦，不煩指顧，不動聲色，而天下遂以大治。何以明其然耶？昔也，時雍于唐，風動于虞，民何以至此極也？遊堯天，戴舜日，彼固無用此贅軍冗賦爲也。所無用者，獨其軍賦哉？兢兢然，業業然，根本之地誠先之也。後及三代，而鋤强取暴，軍
translation_en: … them? Therefore, if one abruptly speaks of showing compassion for the people, the people cannot thereby receive compassion; if one abruptly speaks of [reducing] taxes, taxes cannot thereby be reduced. Only after the military is put in order can one speak of reducing taxes, and only after taxes are reduced can showing compassion for the people be carried out. Hence it is said: the essentials are the pivot, and the boat and oars. Yet even that is not all. The saying goes: "Affairs lie in the four quarters, the essentials lie at the center; when the sage holds fast to the essentials, the four quarters come to render service." This, too, is far from easy. If one who rules over others truly maintains non-action in his heart and holds to supreme rectitude, his great guiding principles will surely be upheld, his minor regulations will surely be extended, his military system will surely be clear, his tax levies will surely be reduced, and his benevolent grace will surely reach all the way down. Otherwise, the more the military is put in order, the more disordered it becomes in reality; what is nominally a reduction of taxes actually makes them more burdensome, and the people see no benefit. This is a case of pursuing the blossoms while severing the roots, forgetting what is great. Hence it is said: operating the pivot so that the door opens and closes, and operating the boat and oars so as to cross the river, depends upon the foundation. When one seeks to grasp the essentials of the realm in order to accomplish the affairs of the realm, does the meaning not lie right here? Knowing this to be so, the ruler of men is earnestly concerned with showing compassion for the people, yet treats military affairs and taxation as urgent, places weight on guiding principles and regulations, and roots them all in the disposition of his mind. When the disposition of the mind is rectified and guiding principles and regulations are established, if we put the military in order in the morning, taxes will be reduced by evening; if we reduce taxes in the evening, the people will revive by morning. Without the trouble of pointing or looking about, without changing one's voice or countenance, the realm thereupon attains great order. How can we make clear that this is so? In antiquity, there was general harmony under Tang [Yao 堯] and transformation as by the wind under Yu [Shun 舜]; how did the people reach such perfection? Roaming beneath the sky of Yao and sheltered under the sun of Shun, they naturally had no use for superfluous troops and redundant taxes. And was it only in military affairs and taxes that they had no such use? Cautious and fearful, attentive and diligent, they truly gave priority to the fundamental ground. Later, coming down to the Three Dynasties, when the strong were weeded out and the violent were seized, military…

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
賦稍稍異矣然而夏之民也寧商之民也清周
之民也清則又何以至此極也軍農夫而賦什
一民不病征也寧獨不病征而已祗德之禹躋
敬之湯執競之武爲之次第施爲其間也由斯
以談心術本也軍賦要也審矣不省賦而恤民
枵腹而求生也不治軍而省賦反鑑而索照也
不正心術立紀綱而談軍賦蔀日冥表而怪言
影之不見也亦大惑矣知有本與要之若彼察
無本與要之若此慨然師二帝之已事由三代
===
之芳規淵乎其無思澹乎其無爲凜乎如履薄
而臨深慓乎若持盈而捧玉罔甘于適罔逸于
遊罔溺志于聲色罔馳心于土木罔狹前人規
罔開後世釁以此陳紀紀必肅以此提綱綱必
振司馬董內方伯治外穈稟之軍不登于籍矣
九賦會徵九式均節朘膏之賦不入于朝矣其
閭閻必且朽貫而藏其父老必且含哺而遊其
農夫市人必且荷鍤而歌其婦人小子必且擊
甕而謠其學士大夫薦紳先生必且褒衣博帶
punctuated: 賦稍稍異矣。然而夏之民也寧，商之民也清，周之民也清，則又何以至此極也？軍農夫而賦什一，民不病征也。寧獨不病征而已，祗德之禹、躋敬之湯、執競之武，爲之次第施爲其間也。由斯以談，心術本也，軍賦要也，審矣。不省賦而恤民，枵腹而求生也；不治軍而省賦，反鑑而索照也；不正心術、立紀綱而談軍賦，蔀日冥表而怪言影之不見也，亦大惑矣。知有本與要之若彼，察無本與要之若此，慨然師二帝之已事，由三代之芳規，淵乎其無思，澹乎其無爲，凜乎如履薄而臨深，慓乎若持盈而捧玉，罔甘于適，罔逸于遊，罔溺志于聲色，罔馳心于土木，罔狹前人規，罔開後世釁。以此陳紀，紀必肅；以此提綱，綱必振。司馬董內，方伯治外，穈稟之軍不登于籍矣；九賦會徵，九式均節，朘膏之賦不入于朝矣。其閭閻必且朽貫而藏，其父老必且含哺而遊，其農夫市人必且荷鍤而歌，其婦人小子必且擊甕而謠，其學士大夫、薦紳先生必且褒衣博帶，
translation_en:
… and taxes became somewhat different. Yet the people of Xia were tranquil, the people of Shang were pure, and the people of Zhou were pure—how then did they also reach such perfection? Soldiers were drawn from farmers and taxes were one-tenth, so the people did not suffer from levies. Nor was it merely that they did not suffer from levies; Yu who revered virtue, Tang who ascended in reverence, and King Wu who held fast to vigor implemented their measures in due order amidst it all. Speaking from this perspective, it is clear that the disposition of the mind is the root, and military and fiscal affairs are the essentials. To show compassion for the people without reducing taxes is to seek survival on an empty stomach; to reduce taxes without regulating the military is to turn a mirror backward and look for a reflection; to discuss military and fiscal affairs without rectifying the disposition of the mind and establishing discipline and order is to screen off the sun, darken the gnomon, and yet wonder why no shadow is seen—this is great delusion indeed!

Knowing how having the root and essentials leads to that result, and observing how lacking the root and essentials leads to this result, one should resolutely take as one's model the accomplished deeds of the Two Emperors and follow the fine regulations of the Three Dynasties: abyssal in having no selfish thoughts, serene in non-action,Awesome as if treading on thin ice and approaching a deep abyss, cautious as if holding a full vessel and carrying jade; never indulging in comfort, never idling in excursions, never drowning the will in music and women, never letting the mind run wild on construction projects, never narrowing the plans of predecessors, and never opening rifts for future generations. Setting forth the lesser threads of governance by this, the threads will surely be solemn; upholding the main cord of governance by this, the cord will surely be invigorated. With the Minister of War supervising the interior and the Regional Earls governing the exterior, soldiers who merely waste grain rations will not be entered on the registers; with the Nine Tributes accounting for revenue and the Nine Formulas equalizing expenditure, taxes that drain the fat and blood of the people will not enter the court. The common folk in the lanes and alleys will surely store away coins on rotting strings; the elders will surely stroll about with food in their mouths; the farmers and townspeople will surely sing while carrying their spades; the women and children will surely chant while tapping on earthen jars; the scholars, grandees, and gentry will surely wear wide robes and broad sashes, …

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
安行徐言而無所却顧熈熈乎穆穆□□□□
以淳風闥八荒如同室斯誠得當唐虞三代哉
乃無異故其所以成務者有要而有本也辟之
工倕作室津人操舟樞運而楫利何窹力焉也
後治卑卑無足語此周衰而降漢唐已逺不逮
至宋而陵替加焉庸可幾乎朱子所以欷歔感
嘆而三致意也彼其内政不脩外侵孔亟安有
天下阽危若是而上不驚者則亦無得于其本
無見于其要焉耳此可謂不知務矣向令端本
===
===
而操要以圖大務何至軍驕食冗賦蹙民窮一
折而入于夷哉故夫朱子之未試其言朱子之
深憂也有天下國家之責者誠得其說而行之
則幾矣
表
擬
御製輔臣賛和詩集序
示大學士楊一清等謝表〔嘉靖七年〕
姜詵
punctuated:
安行徐言，而無所却顧。熈熈乎，穆穆□□□□以淳風，闥八荒如同室，斯誠得當唐、虞、三代哉！乃無異故，其所以成務者，有要而有本也。辟之工倕作室，津人操舟，樞運而楫利，何窹力焉也！後治卑卑，無足語此。周衰而降，漢、唐已逺不逮；至宋而陵替加焉，庸可幾乎？朱子所以欷歔感嘆而三致意也。彼其内政不脩，外侵孔亟，安有天下阽危若是而上不驚者？則亦無得于其本，無見于其要焉耳，此可謂不知務矣。向令端本而操要以圖大務，何至軍驕食冗，賦蹙民窮，一折而入于夷哉？故夫朱子之未試其言，朱子之深憂也。有天下國家之責者，誠得其說而行之，則幾矣。

表
擬御製輔臣賛和詩集序，示大學士楊一清等謝表〔嘉靖七年〕
姜詵
translation_en:
…walk calmly and speak unhurriedly, without having to look back in anxiety. Harmonious and solemn, [? four illegible characters] with pure customs, opening the eight wildest bounds as if they were a single chamber—this would truly match the ages of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties! There is no other reason for this than that the means by which affairs are accomplished possess both the essentials and the fundamentals. Compare it to Artisan Chui building a house or a ferryman steering a boat: when the pivot turns smoothly and the oar moves sharply, what exhausting effort [?] is needed? The governance of later eras was petty and unworthy of being discussed in these terms. From the decline of the Zhou downward, the Han and Tang already fell far short; by the Song, deterioration grew even worse—how could it possibly come close? This is why Master Zhu [Zhu Xi 朱熹] sighed with emotion and repeatedly expressed his concern. In that era, domestic governance was uncultivated and foreign invasions were exceedingly urgent; how could the realm be in such imminent peril without the ruler being alarmed? It was simply that they had not grasped the fundamentals and had no insight into the essentials; this may be called not knowing what business to attend to. Had they rectified the fundamentals and grasped the essentials in planning great affairs, how would it have come to the point where the soldiers were arrogant and rations superfluous, levies urgent and the people impoverished, collapsing at a single blow and falling to the barbarians? Therefore, that Master Zhu's words were never put to the test was Master Zhu's profound sorrow. If those who bear responsibility for the empire and the state truly obtain his teachings and put them into practice, they will be near the mark!

Memorial (Biao)
An Imitation of the Memorial by Grand Secretary Yang Yiqing 楊一清 and Others Giving Thanks for Being Shown the Imperially Composed Preface to the Collection of Poems in Praise and Harmony with the Grand Ministers [7th year of the Jiajing 嘉靖 reign (1528)]
By Jiang Shen 姜詵

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
同考試官訓導龍批頌而典謙道□□□□
得人臣對
君之體且其藻繪不煩莊嚴自在直軼唐宋而上之宜錄以式
考試官敎諭程批抒思微婉摛詞藻麗藹
之當時賡和之意宛然
考試官敎諭周批莊重典則非馳騁浮靡者
嘉靖七年正月某日具官臣楊一清等伏
蒙
聖恩以臣等元旦日恭和
===
御製五言律詩彙爲一冊仍
親序其端名曰輔臣贊和詩集序
頒示臣等臣等誠惶誠恐稽首頓首稱
謝者
皇綸晉錫煥
九重奎璧之章
聖德謙光啓千載地
天之泰采菲葑而罔棄
冠琬琰以增榮拜手祗承靦顏知愧竊惟詩
punctuated:
同考試官訓導龍批：頌而典，謙道□□□□，得人臣對君之體。且其藻繪不煩，莊嚴自在，直軼唐、宋而上之，宜錄以式。
考試官敎諭程批：抒思微婉，摛詞藻麗，藹之當時賡和之意宛然。
考試官敎諭周批：莊重典則，非馳騁浮靡者。
嘉靖七年正月某日，具官臣楊一清等，伏蒙聖恩，以臣等元旦日恭和御製五言律詩彙爲一冊，仍親序其端，名曰《輔臣贊和詩集序》，頒示臣等。臣等誠惶誠恐，稽首頓首稱謝者。
皇綸晉錫，煥九重奎璧之章；聖德謙光，啓千載地天之泰。采菲葑而罔棄，冠琬琰以增榮。拜手祗承，靦顏知愧。竊惟詩
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Assistant Instructor Long comments: Eulogy yet classical, modest in its reasoning […], attaining the proper form of a minister addressing his Sovereign. Moreover, its literary ornament is unburdened, dignified and effortless, directly surpassing the Tang and Song dynasties to reach a higher plane; it ought to be recorded as a model.

Examiner Instructor Cheng comments: It expresses thoughts with subtle grace and unfolds phrases of ornate beauty; the genial spirit of responding in verse at that time is vividly present [?].

Examiner Instructor Zhou comments: Dignified and canonical in standard, not the work of someone given to unrestrained and superficial华麗 extravagance.

On a certain day of the first month of the seventh year of the Jiajing reign [1528], your servants holding full official titles, Yang Yiqing 楊一清 and others, humbly received Your Sacred Grace: taking the five-syllable regulated verses that your servants reverently composed in harmony with the Imperially Composed poem on New Year's Day, You compiled them into a single volume, personally wrote a preface at its head entitled Preface to the Collection of Poems by Grand Secretaries in Harmonious Praise (Fuchen zanhe shiji xu), and promulgated and showed it to your servants. With utmost trepidation and awe, your servants bow our heads to the ground and offer our thanks:

The Imperial words are generously bestowed, shining with the literary brilliance of the constellations from the Ninefold Palace; Your Sacred Virtue shines in modesty, opening up a thousand years of the great peace of Heaven and Earth in harmony. Gathering even turnip and mustard greens without discarding them, You crown them with fine jades to heighten our glory. Bowing with clasped hands, we reverently receive this, our faces flushing with a sense of shame. We humbly reflect that poetry…

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
以言志本治世之麻音頌不忘規惟藎臣
之懿榘道先交儆事匪彌文故虞室賡歌
播喜起明良之盛曁周岡嗣響宣優游泮
渙之和酬唱同聲分靡睽於簾陛贊襄協
德化丕式於寰區自大雅旣湮而末流斯
競興思猛士徒遺馬上之風侈豔祥麟祗
習房中之曲第詩章於三等角技雕蟲直
供奉者五人溺情遊燕屬和薇槐之賦義
奚補於格心賜序蘭菊之篇意豈存于納

作者之謂聖斯美焉而可傳玆蓋恭遇
皇帝陛下
仁孝性成
欽明神授
觀人文以成化運乾旋坤轉之功
