title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
六寸爲坤乃邵子皇極經世聲起于多乾
之甲也音起于古乾之子也此理之可通
于易者也以娶妻生子言之黃鍾爲陽大
呂爲陰猶甲子之娶乙丑皆同位者也黃
鍾之生林鍾林鍾之生太簇猶甲子金之
生庚辰金皆隔八者也乃沈重鍾律議用
京房之術求之得三百六十律當一朞之
日隨日建律依次運行當日者以次爲宮
而商徵以次從焉此義之有符于曆者也
===
樂必用五音然周禮三大祭皆無商音說
者謂周德木也故祭鬼神之樂去金開元
諸臣建言亦謂唐土德王請加商調去角
調是卽周禮之意云耳我
朝以土德王
太祖高皇帝初作洪武正韻聲起于東從角也
後見禮部韻會而遵用之不起于東而起
于公此則從宮矣豈非深達造化者哉律
止于十二是矣然十二者律之本聲而四
punctuated: 六寸爲坤。乃邵子《皇極經世》聲起于多，乾之甲也；音起于古，乾之子也。此理之可通于《易》者也。以娶妻生子言之：黃鍾爲陽，大呂爲陰，猶甲子之娶乙丑，皆同位者也；黃鍾之生林鍾，林鍾之生太簇，猶甲子金之生庚辰金，皆隔八者也。乃沈重《鍾律議》用京房之術求之，得三百六十律，當一朞之日，隨日建律，依次運行，當日者以次爲宮，而商、徵以次從焉。此義之有符于曆者也。樂必用五音，然《周禮》三大祭皆無商音。說者謂周德木也，故祭鬼神之樂去金。開元諸臣建言，亦謂唐土德王，請加商調，去角調，是卽《周禮》之意云耳。我朝以土德王，太祖高皇帝初作《洪武正韻》，聲起于東，從角也；後見《禮部韻會》而遵用之，不起于東而起于公，此則從宮矣，豈非深達造化者哉！律止于十二，是矣。然十二者，律之本聲；而四…
translation_en: … is six inches long and represents Kun. Moreover, in Master Shao’s [Shao Yong 邵雍] Supreme Principles Governing the World (Huangji jingshi), the finals (sheng) begin with “duo,” which corresponds to the first Heaven Stem (jia) of Qian, while the initials (yin) begin with “gu,” which corresponds to the first Earth Branch (zi) of Qian. This is how the principle of pitch pipes connects with the Book of Changes (Yi). Speaking in terms of “marrying a wife and begetting sons”: Yellow Bell (Huangzhong) is yang and Great Regulator (Dalü) is yin, which is like jiazi marrying yichou, both occupying the same position; Yellow Bell begets Forest Bell (Linzhong), and Forest Bell begets Great Cluster (Taicu), which is like the metal of jiazi begetting the metal of gengchen, each separated by eight positions. Furthermore, Shen Zhong’s Discourse on Bell Pitch Pipes (Zhonglü yi) applied the method of Jing Fang to calculate them, obtaining three hundred and sixty pitch pipes corresponding to the days of a full year. As each day establishes its pitch pipe and they circulate in sequence, the pipe governing the day serves in turn as the gong note, while shang and zhi follow in order. This is how their meaning accords with the calendar. Music must employ the five tones, yet in the Rites of Zhou (Zhouli) the three great sacrifices all lack the shang tone. Commentators explain that the virtue of the Zhou dynasty was Wood, and therefore the music for sacrificing to ghosts and spirits omitted Metal [the element corresponding to shang]. During the Kaiyuan era [713–741], various officials submitted proposals arguing likewise that since the Tang dynasty ruled by the virtue of Earth, the shang mode should be added and the jue mode [corresponding to Wood] removed—which was simply following the intent of the Rites of Zhou. Our Dynasty rules by the virtue of Earth. When Emperor Gao, our Grand Progenitor (Taizu), first compiled the Correct Rhymes of the Hongwu Era (Hongwu zhengyun), the rhymes began with “dong,” thus following the jue tone. Later, upon seeing the Collection of Rhymes of the Ministry of Rites (Libu yunhui), he adopted and followed it, beginning not with “dong” but with “gong,” thereby following the gong tone [corresponding to Earth]. Was this not a profound comprehension of the workings of nature! That the pitch pipes stop at twelve is indeed true. Yet the twelve are the fundamental sounds of the pitch pipes, whereas the four…

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
者應聲也本聲重大爲君爲父應聲輕清
爲臣爲子故四聲曰清聲卽夾鐘大呂黃
鐘太簇之應也苟不用四清聲是有本而
無應矣我
朝泠謙建議用四清聲故編鐘編磬皆爲十
六豈非洞達音律者哉詩稱定之方中謂
測日景以辨方也土圭之法祖冲之之論
備矣然候氣者使按日景之子午以布律
則氣必不應何也天氣微偏于左地氣微
===
偏于右所謂不參差則不能生物者也故
土圭測日景常在子午之中此天之正位
也以鍼定南北常在丙午壬子之中此地
之正位也故冬至置黃鐘之律于壬子之
中夏至置林鐘之律于丙午之中然後飛
灰應律今元定乃欲一室之中多截管以
候黃鐘夫差之毫釐氣卽不應而顧欲多
埋律管豈非臆說哉黃鐘起于子之一以
三倍之歷十二辰而終于亥之一十七萬
punctuated: 者，應聲也。本聲重大，爲君、爲父；應聲輕清，爲臣、爲子。故四聲曰清聲，卽夾鐘、大呂、黃鐘、太簇之應也。苟不用四清聲，是有本而無應矣。我朝泠謙建議用四清聲，故編鐘、編磬皆爲十六，豈非洞達音律者哉！《詩》稱「定之方中」，謂測日景以辨方也。土圭之法，祖冲之之論備矣。然候氣者，使按日景之子午以布律，則氣必不應。何也？天氣微偏于左，地氣微偏于右，所謂不參差則不能生物者也。故土圭測日景，常在子午之中，此天之正位也；以鍼定南北，常在丙午、壬子之中，此地之正位也。故冬至置黃鐘之律于壬子之中，夏至置林鐘之律于丙午之中，然後飛灰應律。今元定乃欲一室之中多截管以候黃鐘。夫差之毫釐，氣卽不應，而顧欲多埋律管，豈非臆說哉！黃鐘起于子之一，以三倍之，歷十二辰，而終于亥之一十七萬
translation_en:
… four are the responding tones. The fundamental tones are heavy and grand, serving as ruler and father; the responding tones are light and clear, serving as minister and son. Therefore, these four tones are called the "clear tones" (qingsheng), which are namely the responses to Jiazhong, Dalü, Huangzhong, and Taicu. If the four clear tones were not used, there would be fundamentals without responses. In our dynasty, Ling Qian 泠謙 proposed using the four clear tones, so the sets of chime bells (bianzhong) and stone chimes (bianqing) were both made to consist of sixteen pieces—was he not one who thoroughly understood musical acoustics and pitch pipes?

The Book of Odes (Shi) speaks of "when the star Ding was in the middle of the sky," referring to measuring the sun's shadow in order to determine orientation. Regarding the method of the shadow-measuring gnomon (tugui), Zu Chongzhi's 祖冲之 discussion of it is comprehensive. However, for those who watch for the seasonal ethers (houqi), if they were to arrange the pitch pipes according to the north-south (zi-wu) axis of the sun's shadow, the ethers would certainly not respond. Why is this? The ether of Heaven inclines slightly to the left, and the ether of Earth inclines slightly to the right—this is what is meant by "without slight divergence, living things cannot be generated." Therefore, when the gnomon measures the sun's shadow, it is always centered on the due north-south axis of zi and wu; this is the true position of Heaven. When a magnetic needle is used to determine south and north, it is always centered between bing-wu and ren-zi; this is the true position of Earth. Consequently, at the winter solstice one places the pitch pipe of Huangzhong at the center of ren-zi, and at the summer solstice one places the pitch pipe of Linzhong at the center of bing-wu; only then will the blown ashes respond to the pitch pipes. Now Cai Yuanding 蔡元定 instead wanted to cut many pipes within a single chamber to await the response of Huangzhong. Now, if there is an error of even a hair's breadth, the ether will not respond; yet to wish instead to bury numerous pitch pipes—is that not mere conjecture?

Huangzhong begins with one at zi; multiplying it by three successively through the twelve earthly branches (chen), it ends at hai with one hundred seventy…

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
七千一百四十七漢志蓋借十二辰以列
三因之筭位耳故有寸分釐毫絲之法有
寸分釐毫絲之數至章明也蔡子不知其
假借立法而以爲真有十二辰之數張皇
鋪衍而去真益遠矣自黃鐘之管陽皆下
生陰皆上生自蕤賓之管陽反上生陰反
下生此非空言也從子至巳陽生陰退故
律生呂言下生呂生律言上生從午至亥
陰生陽退故律生呂言上生呂生律言下
===
生蓋班志隔八相生一下一上則終于仲
呂其長止三寸三分有奇京房之法至蕤
賓重上生凡五下六上終于仲呂其長六
寸六分有奇若仲呂止三寸三分有奇雖
三分益一不能復生黃鐘之律故用六寸
六分則三分益一可以復生黃鐘耳蔡子
乃譏其陰陽錯亂毋亦未之思乎雖然此
猶可也近世儒者乃又倡爲之說曰黃鐘
非九寸之管而引外紀呂氏春秋所載舍
punctuated: 七千一百四十七。《漢志》蓋借十二辰以列三因之筭位耳。故有寸、分、釐、毫、絲之法，有寸、分、釐、毫、絲之數，至章明也。蔡子不知其假借立法，而以爲真有十二辰之數，張皇鋪衍，而去真益遠矣。自黃鐘之管，陽皆下生，陰皆上生；自蕤賓之管，陽反上生，陰反下生，此非空言也。從子至巳，陽生陰退，故律生呂言下生，呂生律言上生；從午至亥，陰生陽退，故律生呂言上生，呂生律言下生。蓋班《志》隔八相生，一下一上，則終于仲呂，其長止三寸三分有奇。京房之法，至蕤賓重上生，凡五下六上，終于仲呂，其長六寸六分有奇。若仲呂止三寸三分有奇，雖三分益一，不能復生黃鐘之律；故用六寸六分，則三分益一可以復生黃鐘耳。蔡子乃譏其陰陽錯亂，毋亦未之思乎？雖然，此猶可也。近世儒者乃又倡爲之說曰：「黃鐘非九寸之管。」而引《外紀》、《呂氏春秋》所載舍
translation_en:
…7,147. The Treatise in the Book of Han (Hanzhi) merely borrowed the twelve earthly branches to arrange the places for the calculation of multiplication by three. Thus, there is the method of inches (cun), tenths (fen), hundredths (li), thousandths (hao), and ten-thousandths (si), and there are the numerical values for inches, tenths, hundredths, thousandths, and ten-thousandths, which is utterly clear and evident. Master Cai [Cai Yuanding 蔡元定] did not realize that this was a borrowed convention to establish a method, and instead believed that there truly were numerical values inherent in the twelve earthly branches; he magnified and elaborated upon it, straying ever further from the truth.

Starting from the pitch-pipe of Huangzhong, the yang pitches all generate downward [by subtracting one-third] and the yin pitches all generate upward [by adding one-third]; starting from the pitch-pipe of Ruibin, the yang pitches conversely generate upward and the yin pitches conversely generate downward. This is no empty talk. From zi to si, yang grows and yin recedes; therefore, when a yang pitch (lü) generates a yin pitch (lü), it is called downward generation, and when a yin pitch generates a yang pitch, it is called upward generation. From wu to hai, yin grows and yang recedes; therefore, when a yang pitch generates a yin pitch, it is called upward generation, and when a yin pitch generates a yang pitch, it is called downward generation. Now, in Ban Gu's Treatise (Banzhi), where pitches generate one another at every eighth position by alternating one downward and one upward generation, the cycle ends at Zhonglü, whose length is only three inches, three tenths, and a fraction. According to Jing Fang's method, upon reaching Ruibin it repeats an upward generation, making five downward and six upward generations in all, and ends at Zhonglü with a length of six inches, six tenths, and a fraction. If Zhonglü were only three inches, three tenths, and a fraction, even by adding one-third to its length it could not regenerate the pitch of Huangzhong; therefore, by using six inches and six tenths, adding one-third allows it to regenerate Huangzhong. Master Cai nonetheless criticized this as throwing yin and yang into confusion—had he not failed to think it through?

Even so, this much is still tolerable. Yet scholars of recent times have further championed a theory claiming, "Huangzhong is not a nine-inch pipe," citing the Outer Annals (Waiji) and the Spring and Autumn Annals of Master Lü (Lüshi chunqiu), which record the… [han/she 舍 for 含]…

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
少之說爲証曰黃鐘音始也象則君也其
律宜短其氣宜微其聲宜清者也是知其
一而不知其二者也夫黃鐘以八十一分
爲管而吹三十九分以爲聲故謂之含少
乃遂以三十九分爲黃鐘之律而執含少
以爲清管焉是其言本非誤而所以信其
言者誤矣此律一差大呂而下十一律者
將無由取正矣何其好爲異論而不師古
哉蓋太史公之言曰細若氣微若聲聖人
===
神而明之雖妙必效彼氣之嬴縮聲之清
濁固有不在于器數之末者使誠在于器
數之末也烏用是聖人神明爲哉雖然審
律之道神解爲上得數者次之不求律于
心而求律于器最下矣毋論黍之縱橫尺
之長短愚直謂俗樂與雅樂亦不甚懸絕
者夫金石鐘磬也後世易之爲方響絲竹
琴簫也後世易之爲箏笛此雅樂之變爲
俗樂者也黃鐘用合字大呂太簇用四字
punctuated: 少之說爲証，曰：「黃鐘，音始也，象則君也；其律宜短，其氣宜微，其聲宜清者也。」是知其一而不知其二者也。夫黃鐘以八十一分爲管，而吹三十九分以爲聲，故謂之含少；乃遂以三十九分爲黃鐘之律，而執含少以爲清管焉。是其言本非誤，而所以信其言者誤矣。此律一差，大呂而下十一律者，將無由取正矣。何其好爲異論而不師古哉！蓋太史公之言曰：「細若氣，微若聲，聖人神而明之，雖妙必效。」彼氣之嬴縮、聲之清濁，固有不在于器數之末者。使誠在于器數之末也，烏用是聖人神明爲哉！雖然，審律之道，神解爲上，得數者次之，不求律于心而求律于器，最下矣。毋論黍之縱橫、尺之長短，愚直謂俗樂與雅樂亦不甚懸絕者。夫金石，鐘磬也，後世易之爲方響；絲竹，琴簫也，後世易之爲箏笛：此雅樂之變爲俗樂者也。黃鐘用合字，大呂、太簇用四字，
translation_en: … the theory of "holding the lesser" (hanshao) as evidence, saying: "Yellow Bell (Huangzhong) is the beginning of sound, and its image is that of the ruler; its pitch-pipe should be short, its vital breath subtle, and its sound clear." This is to know one aspect while remaining ignorant of the other. Now, Yellow Bell uses eighty-one fen for its pipe, while thirty-nine fen are blown to produce its sound, which is why it is called "holding the lesser." Yet they thereupon take thirty-nine fen to be the pitch-pipe of Yellow Bell itself, clinging to "holding the lesser" to make it a high, clear pipe. Thus the original statement itself was not mistaken, but the way they believed and interpreted it was mistaken. Once this foundational pitch errs, the eleven pitches from Great Regulator (Dalü) downward will have no means of being rectified. How fond they are of making heterodox arguments instead of taking antiquity as their teacher! Indeed, the Grand Historian (Taishigong, Sima Qian) said: "Subtle as vital breath, faint as sound—the sage comprehends and illuminates it through spirit; though marvelous, it is surely verified." That waxing and waning of vital breath, and the clarity and turbidity of sound, truly do not lie in the trivialities of instruments and numbers. If they really lay in the trivialities of instruments and numbers, what need would there be for the spiritual illumination of the sage? Even so, in the way of examining the pitches, spiritual comprehension is highest, grasping the numbers comes next, and not seeking the pitches in the mind but seeking them in instruments is the lowest of all. Setting aside whether the millet grains are arranged lengthwise or crosswise, or whether the foot-measure is long or short, I would simply say that popular music (suyue) and elegant court music (yayue) are not so vastly separated from one another. Now, metal and stone mean bells and chime-stones, which later ages replaced with iron metallophones (fangxiang); silk and bamboo mean zithers (qin) and panpipes (xiao), which later ages replaced with bridged zithers (zheng) and transverse flutes (di)—this is how elegant music changed into popular music. Yellow Bell uses the gongche notation character "he", Great Regulator and Great Cluster (Taicu) use the character "si", …

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
夾鍾姑洗用一字夷則南呂用工字此俗
樂之可通于雅樂者也微獨此古以俎豆
今以盃盂古以莞席今以案榻雖聖人復
生不能舍盃盂而復俎豆棄案榻而用莞
席也是古今音樂之說也雖然此之謂樂
器爾數爾非所論于器與數之外也夫有
器而無官與無器同知聲而不知音知音
而不知樂與無官同舍其本而圖其末沾
沾焉鐘律是較非樂之完也本立矣末其
===
矣天造未寧而極音以逞非樂之至也蓋
聲如味一氣二體三類四物五聲六律七
音八風九歌以相成也清濁小大短長疾
徐哀樂剛柔遲速高下出入周疏以相濟
也是樂之器也記所謂聽其鏗鏘者也子
野歌而南北之風殊伯牙鼓琴而峩峩洋
洋之音著后夔氏典樂八音諧神人和焉
是樂之官也記所謂審音以知樂者也嗣
是而後荀勗之識牛鐸阮咸之較玉尺張
punctuated: 夾鍾、姑洗用一字，夷則、南呂用工字，此俗樂之可通于雅樂者也。微獨此，古以俎豆，今以盃盂；古以莞席，今以案榻。雖聖人復生，不能舍盃盂而復俎豆，棄案榻而用莞席也。是古今音樂之說也。雖然，此之謂樂器爾、數爾，非所論于器與數之外也。夫有器而無官，與無器同；知聲而不知音，知音而不知樂，與無官同。舍其本而圖其末，沾沾焉鐘律是較，非樂之完也。本立矣，末其矣，天造未寧而極音以逞，非樂之至也。蓋聲如味：一氣、二體、三類、四物、五聲、六律、七音、八風、九歌，以相成也；清濁、小大、短長、疾徐、哀樂、剛柔、遲速、高下、出入、周疏，以相濟也。是樂之器也，《記》所謂「聽其鏗鏘」者也。子野歌而南北之風殊，伯牙鼓琴而峩峩洋洋之音著，后夔氏典樂，八音諧，神人和焉。是樂之官也，《記》所謂「審音以知樂」者也。嗣是而後，荀勗之識牛鐸，阮咸之較玉尺，張
translation_en: …Jiazhong and Guxian use the note yi, while Yize and Nanlü use the note gong; this is how popular music can be connected with elegant music. Nor is this the only instance: in antiquity people used sacrificial stands and stemmed bowls (zudou), whereas today they use cups and basins; in antiquity they used rush mats, whereas today they use tables and couches. Even if a sage were to be reborn, he could not abandon cups and basins to restore sacrificial stands and stemmed bowls, nor discard tables and couches to use rush mats. Such is the explanation of ancient and modern music. Even so, what has been discussed here refers merely to musical instruments and numerical proportions, not to what lies beyond instruments and proportions. Indeed, to possess the instruments without the auditory faculty (guan) is the same as having no instruments at all; to know mere sounds (sheng) without knowing musical tones (yin), and to know tones without knowing music (yue), is the same as having no auditory faculty. To abandon the root and pursue the branches, busying oneself complacently with comparing bells and pitch-pipes, is not the perfection of music. When the root is established and the branches [follow?], yet the workings of Heaven are not yet at peace and one indulges in extreme sounds for self-gratification, this is not the ultimate attainment of music. For sound is like flavor: the one vital breath, the two styles of dance, the three poetic categories, the four material sources from the four quarters, the five notes, the six pitch-standards, the seven tones, the eight winds, and the nine songs complement one another; clear and turbid, small and large, short and long, rapid and gradual, mournful and joyful, firm and yielding, slow and fast, high and low, entering and exiting, dense and sparse balance one another. These are the instruments of music—what the Record of Music calls "listening to their ringing and clanging." When Ziye (Music Master Kuang) sang, the airs of north and south were distinguished; when Boya played the zither, the tones of lofty mountains and vast waters were made manifest; when Minister Kui (Hou Kui) was Director of Music, the eight timbres were in harmony and spirits and men were brought into accord. This is the auditory faculty of music—what the Record of Music calls "examining tones in order to understand music." Thereafter, Xun Xu's recognition of the cow-bell, Ruan Xian's calibration of the jade foot-rule, Zhang…

夾鐘姑洗用一字夷則南呂用工字此俗
樂之可通于雅樂者也微獨此古以俎豆
今以盃盂古以莞席今以案榻雖聖人復
生不能舍盃盂而復俎豆棄案榻而用莞
席也是古今音樂之說也雖然此之謂樂
器爾數爾非所論于器與數之外也夫有
器而無官與無器同知聲而不知音知音
而不知樂與無官同舍其本而圖其末沾
沾焉鐘律是較非樂之完也本立矣末其
===
矣天造未寧而極音以逞非樂之至也蓋
聲如味一氣二體三類四物五聲六律七
音八風九歌以相成也清濁小大短長疾
徐哀樂剛柔遲速高下出入周疏以相濟
也是樂之器也記所謂聽其鏗鏘者也子
野歌而南北之風殊伯牙鼓琴而峩峩洋
洋之音著后夔氏典樂八音諧神人和焉
是樂之官也記所謂審音以知樂者也嗣
是而後荀勗之識牛鐸阮咸之較玉尺張
punctuated: 夾鐘、姑洗用「一」字，夷則、南呂用「工」字，此俗樂之可通于雅樂者也。微獨此，古以俎豆，今以盃盂；古以莞席，今以案榻。雖聖人復生，不能舍盃盂而復俎豆，棄案榻而用莞席也。是古今音樂之說也。雖然，此之謂樂器爾，數爾，非所論于器與數之外也。夫有器而無官，與無器同；知聲而不知音，知音而不知樂，與無官同。舍其本而圖其末，沾沾焉鐘律是較，非樂之完也。本立矣，末其矣。天造未寧，而極音以逞，非樂之至也。蓋聲如味，一氣、二體、三類、四物、五聲、六律、七音、八風、九歌，以相成也；清濁、小大、短長、疾徐、哀樂、剛柔、遲速、高下、出入、周疏，以相濟也。是樂之器也，《記》所謂「聽其鏗鏘」者也。子野歌而南北之風殊，伯牙鼓琴而峩峩洋洋之音著，后夔氏典樂，八音諧，神人和焉，是樂之官也，《記》所謂「審音以知樂」者也。嗣是而後，荀勗之識牛鐸，阮咸之較玉尺，張
translation_en: … Jiazhong and Guxian correspond to the note yi, and Yize and Nanlü correspond to the note gong; this shows how popular music can be correlated with court music. Nor is this the only case: antiquity used sacrificial stands and platters (zudou), whereas today we use cups and bowls; antiquity used rush mats, whereas today we use tables and couches. Even if a sage were born again, he could not abandon cups and bowls to restore sacrificial stands and platters, or discard tables and couches to use rush mats. This is the theory of ancient and modern music. Even so, what has been discussed here is merely the instruments of music and its mathematical proportions; it does not address what lies beyond instruments and proportions. Now, to have instruments without a discerning ear is the same as having no instruments at all; to know sounds (sheng) without knowing tones (yin), and to know tones without knowing music (yue), is the same as having no discerning ear. To abandon the root and pursue the branches, complacently busying oneself with calibrating bells and pitch-pipes, is not the perfection of music. Once the root is established, the branches [will follow (?)]; when the state of the realm is not yet at peace, to indulge in extreme sounds is not the ultimate of music. Indeed, sound is like flavor: the one vital breath (qi), the two forms of dance, the three poetic categories, the four materials from the four quarters, the five notes, the six pitch-standards, the seven tones, the eight winds, and the nine songs complement one another; clear and turbid, small and large, short and long, rapid and gradual, mournful and joyful, firm and yielding, slow and fast, high and low, entering and exiting, dense and sparse balance one another. These are the instruments of music—what the Record of Music calls "listening to their ringing and clanging." When Ziye (Shi Kuang) sang, he distinguished the airs of North and South; when Bo Ya played the zither (qin), the sounds of lofty mountains and vast waters were made manifest; when Lord Kui (Hou Kui) was Director of Music, the eight timbres were in harmony and spirits and men were brought into accord. This is the discerning faculty of music—what the Record of Music calls "examining tones in order to understand music." title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
文收得玉磬而知黃鐘之缺楊收見古鐘
而定姑洗之角之數子者是亦樂之官也
記所謂審聲以知音者也昔者吳公子札
聘魯請觀周樂工爲之舞武曰美哉周之
盛也爲之舞濩曰聖人之弘也猶有慚德
爲之舞夏曰美哉勤而不德者也爲之舞
韶曰德至矣哉如天之幬如地之載雖甚
盛德蔑以加矣此數聖人者如察秋毫如
較累黍不少爽焉豈樂固有本耶何按遺
===
音于數千載後而歷歷如睹也此樂之完
也嘗攷其時敷文德舞干羽有苗格而韶
作歸馬放牛示弗服用垂拱無爲而武作
蓋聖人治定制禮功成作樂自六代而已
然矣故曰樂以安德義以處之禮以行之
信以守之仁以厲之而後可以殿邦國同
福祿來遠人所謂樂也此樂之至也方今
承平二百餘年百官序萬事理榮問鬯和
氣翔是虞夏之盛也可謂有其時矣
punctuated:
文收得玉磬而知黃鐘之缺，楊收見古鐘而定姑洗之角；之數子者，是亦樂之官也，《記》所謂「審聲以知音」者也。昔者吳公子札聘魯，請觀周樂。工爲之舞《武》，曰：「美哉！周之盛也。」爲之舞《濩》，曰：「聖人之弘也，猶有慚德。」爲之舞《夏》，曰：「美哉！勤而不德者也。」爲之舞《韶》，曰：「德至矣哉！如天之幬，如地之載；雖甚盛德，蔑以加矣。」此數聖人者，如察秋毫，如較累黍，不少爽焉。豈樂固有本耶？何按遺音于數千載後，而歷歷如睹也？此樂之完也。

嘗攷其時：敷文德，舞干羽，有苗格而《韶》作；歸馬放牛，示弗服用，垂拱無爲而《武》作。蓋聖人治定制禮，功成作樂，自六代而已然矣。故曰：「樂以安德，義以處之，禮以行之，信以守之，仁以厲之，而後可以殿邦國，同福祿，來遠人，所謂樂也。」此樂之至也。方今承平二百餘年，百官序，萬事理，榮問鬯，和氣翔，是虞、夏之盛也，可謂有其時矣。
translation_en:
… [Zhang] Wenshou 張文收 obtained a jade chime and knew that the huangzhong pitch was missing, and Yang Shou 楊收 saw an ancient bell and determined that it corresponded to the jue note of the guxian pitch. These several masters also represent the office of music, corresponding to what the Record of Music (Yueji) calls "examining sounds in order to understand tones." In antiquity, Prince Zha 公子札 of Wu 吳 went on a diplomatic mission to Lu 魯 and requested to observe the music of Zhou 周. When the musicians performed the dance of the Wu 武 for him, he said: "How splendid! It is the flourishing of Zhou." When they performed the dance of the Hu 濩 for him, he said: "How broad is the sage! Yet he still feels shame in his virtue." When they performed the dance of the Xia 夏 for him, he said: "How splendid! He toiled tirelessly and yet did not boast of his virtue." When they performed the dance of the Shao 韶 for him, he said: "Virtue has reached its pinnacle! Like heaven that covers all, like earth that sustains all—even the most flourishing virtue could add nothing more to this." In judging these several sages, it was like discerning the tip of an autumn hair or measuring stacked grains of millet, without the slightest error. Does music not indeed have a fundamental root? Otherwise, how could one examine its lingering tones thousands of years later and see everything as clearly as if before one's own eyes? This is the perfection of music.

If we examine those times: when civil virtue was spread and the shield and feather dances were performed, the ruler of Miao 有苗 submitted and the Shao was composed; when horses were sent back and cattle set free to show they would never again be used for war, the ruler let his robes hang down and governed through non-action, and the Wu was composed. Indeed, that the sages established rites when order was secured, and created music when meritorious achievements were completed, had already been the case since the Six Dynasties. Therefore it is said: "Music is used toGive peace to virtue; righteousness to handle affairs; rites to put them into practice; trustworthiness to preserve them; and benevolence to encourage them. Only then can one stabilize the states, share blessings and emoluments, and attract people from afar—this is what is meant by music." This is the culmination of music. At the present time, peace has been inherited for more than two hundred years; the hundred officials are in order, the myriad affairs are well-governed, glorious renown spreads far and wide, and harmonious vital energy soars aloft. This is the flourishing of Yu 虞 and Xia, and it may truly be said that we have the right time for it…

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
爲理之術有三太上化之其次風之其下
聽之章軌物慎樞機所以化之也簡脩別
慝以爲表率所以風之也廉其弗率而謀
其不協訒訒焉無于誰責所以聽之也夫
王者制國固將化之化之不得而求所以
風之則莫先于民之所視民之所視必有
以鉅望而峻責之天下之人比肩而立接
踵而至漫無辨別有善焉而不見其可慕
有不善焉而不見其可惡人主不察而以
===
其法制束縛用之於無所重輕之人索之
愈急而應之愈緩何則此未足以聳動其
心而更易其慮也是所謂治之不協而直
聽之者也天下有人焉其所自處儼然有
以異於常人上之人見以爲異而優之下
之人不敢跂足而望也則世所號爲士者
也凡若人者必其平居舉止軌于度而宅
於理無頗僻恣肆以忝名教夫然後民則
而象之儀而憲之而王者之風聲教澤率
punctuated: 爲理之術有三：太上化之，其次風之，其下聽之。章軌物，慎樞機，所以化之也；簡脩別慝，以爲表率，所以風之也；廉其弗率，而謀其不協，訒訒焉無于誰責，所以聽之也。夫王者制國，固將化之；化之不得，而求所以風之，則莫先于民之所視。民之所視，必有以鉅望而峻責之。天下之人，比肩而立，接踵而至，漫無辨別，有善焉而不見其可慕，有不善焉而不見其可惡；人主不察，而以其法制束縛，用之於無所重輕之人，索之愈急，而應之愈緩。何則？此未足以聳動其心，而更易其慮也。是所謂治之不協，而直聽之者也。天下有人焉，其所自處，儼然有以異於常人；上之人見以爲異而優之，下之人不敢跂足而望也，則世所號爲「士」者也。凡若人者，必其平居舉止，軌于度而宅於理，無頗僻恣肆以忝名教。夫然後民則而象之，儀而憲之，而王者之風聲教澤，率…
translation_en:
There are three methods of governance: the highest is to transform them, the next is to influence them through moral example, and the lowest is to adjudicate them. Making clear the standards and norms and exercising caution over the pivotal springs of action—this is the means to transform them. Selecting the cultivated and distinguishing the wicked so as to serve as models—this is the means to influence them. Investigating those who do not comply and dealing with those who do not harmonize, speaking with hesitant difficulty and having no one upon whom to place true responsibility—this is the means to adjudicate them.

Now, when a true king orders the state, he certainly intends to transform them. If transforming them cannot be achieved, and he seeks the means to influence them, then nothing takes precedence over that toward which the people look. That toward which the people look must be met with great expectations and stern responsibilities. If the people of the realm stand shoulder to shoulder and arrive on each other's heels without any distinction—so that when there is goodness, nothing is seen as worthy of admiration, and when there is evil, nothing is seen as worthy of detestation—and the ruler, failing to discern this, applies his legal regulations and restraints to people who carry neither weight nor consequence, the more urgently he demands of them, the more sluggishly they will respond. Why is this? Because this is insufficient to stir their hearts and alter their thoughts. This is what is meant by governing without harmony and merely adjudicating them.

Yet there are people in the world who conduct themselves with a dignified bearing distinct from ordinary folk. Those above see them as distinct and treat them with favor, while those below dare not even stand on tiptoe to look up to them—these are the ones the world calls "scholars" (shi 士). All such men must, in their ordinary conduct and demeanor, conform to the proper measure and abide in principle, free of partiality, perversity, or unbridled license that would disgrace the moral teachings (mingjiao 名教). Only then will the common people take them as models and imitate them, look to them as patterns and follow their example, and the moral influence and civilizing grace of the true king will entirely…

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
賴以維持於不墜不然民將曰某士也若
是頗僻也某士也若是恣肆也其又何責
夫匹夫畊築而負販者乎故曰莫先於民
之所視民之所視必有以鉅望而峻責之
夫所謂鉅望而峻責之者何也蓋昔者成
周之制得之矣今攷周禮一書其間摹畫
厝注最備且悉總之因其性不拂其宜緣
飾之以法制矯其所偏枉要之於中正如
是而已矣是故其相際也三詔而後通五
===
贄以為見則可謂已飾矣其選授也三物
以為賓再論而後官則可謂已靳矣其省
戒也以八法辨治以六敘正吏則可謂已
察矣夫紹贄以防瀆也物論以杜濫也法
敘以秩能也三者帝王所以章軌宏化而
總人羣之道也故為之士者率其教繇其
制循循焉入於其中瞿然而與之俱化也
言出而為程行出而為度功成名立而民
以為楷式天下之人苟其頑愚顓蒙不至
punctuated: 賴以維持於不墜。不然，民將曰：「某，士也，若是頗僻也；某，士也，若是恣肆也。」其又何責夫匹夫畊築而負販者乎？故曰：莫先於民之所視。民之所視，必有以鉅望而峻責之。夫所謂鉅望而峻責之者，何也？蓋昔者成周之制得之矣。今攷《周禮》一書，其間摹畫厝注，最備且悉。總之，因其性，不拂其宜，緣飾之以法制，矯其所偏枉，要之於中正，如是而已矣。是故其相際也，三詔而後通，五贄以為見，則可謂已飾矣；其選授也，三物以為賓，再論而後官，則可謂已靳矣；其省戒也，以八法辨治，以六敘正吏，則可謂已察矣。夫紹贄以防瀆也，物論以杜濫也，法敘以秩能也，三者帝王所以章軌宏化而總人羣之道也。故為之士者，率其教，繇其制，循循焉入於其中，瞿然而與之俱化也。言出而為程，行出而為度，功成名立而民以為楷式。天下之人，苟其頑愚顓蒙不至
translation_en: … relies upon them to be maintained without falling into decline. Otherwise, the common people will say: "So-and-so is a scholar, yet he is this biased and perverse; so-and-so is a scholar, yet he is this unbridled and licentious." How then could one demand anything of ordinary men who plow, build, and peddle goods on their backs? Therefore, it is said that nothing takes precedence over those whom the people look up to. Toward those whom the people look up to, one must place great expectations and make strict demands. Now, what is meant by placing great expectations and making strict demands upon them? In antiquity, the institutions of the flourishing Zhou dynasty achieved this. If we now examine the Rites of Zhou (Zhouli), the planning and arrangements therein are most complete and detailed. In sum, they followed human nature without going against what was appropriate, adorned it with laws and regulations, corrected its biases and crookedness, and brought it to equilibrium and rectitude—nothing more than this. Therefore, in their social intercourse, they were announced thrice by intermediaries before being introduced and presented five kinds of ceremonial gifts when meeting, which may be called thoroughly refined; in their selection and appointment, they were received as guests on the basis of the Three Matters and evaluated twice before being granted office, which may be called thoroughly circumspect; in their inspection and admonition, governance was distinguished by the Eight Laws and officials were rectified by the Six Orders, which may be called thoroughly discerning. Mediated introductions and ceremonial gifts were to prevent familiarity and disrespect; the Three Matters and evaluations were to stop unworthy appointments; the Eight Laws and Six Orders were to rank ability. These three were the Way by which emperors and kings manifested standards, broadened moral transformation, and governed human society. Thus, those who were scholars followed their teachings and abided by their institutions, entering into them step by step and being awed into transforming along with them. When their words went forth, they became standards; when their actions went forth, they became measures; when their achievements were completed and their reputations established, the common people took them as models. Among the people of the world, so long as their obstinacy, foolishness, and ignorance did not reach the point of …

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
如鳥獸夷虜之不可以人理齒者亦孰不
灑滌磨礱以求不棄於人士之列故當是
時士之自處也甚高而天下之視士也甚
尊其斂容者以陳禮也其戢武者以蹈義
也其兢兢乎法制教令者以明有上而不
敢專也昔人有言無罪以當貴清貞以自
娛周之士所爲貴者以此也至秦則不然
絀儒崇伯而上首功縱橫者鶩揣摩者庸
視舌者進裹足者退以故一切功名之士
===
鼓吻掉臂立談而取卿相其一時氣勢豈
不烜灼然而徐察其所以爲術迺有大謬
不然者吹竽彈鋏要庭呼闥卽廝隸之役
弗旬於此矣投機瞰隙匿情更說卽穿窬
之跡弗垢於此矣摺體伏溺希旨承顏卽
妾婦之容弗媿於此矣夫三者至賤辱也
至亡行也而士乃甘心焉試之以七尺之
軀何也彼見夫左繩右墨者之擯於時而
高議闊談者足以踞要樞也彼見夫廉貞
punctuated: 如鳥獸夷虜之不可以人理齒者，亦孰不灑滌磨礱，以求不棄於人士之列？故當是時，士之自處也甚高，而天下之視士也甚尊。其斂容者，以陳禮也；其戢武者，以蹈義也；其兢兢乎法制教令者，以明有上而不敢專也。昔人有言：「無罪以當貴，清貞以自娛。」周之士所爲貴者，以此也。至秦則不然。絀儒崇伯，而上首功；縱橫者鶩，揣摩者庸，視舌者進，裹足者退。以故一切功名之士，鼓吻掉臂，立談而取卿相，其一時氣勢，豈不烜灼？然而徐察其所以爲術，迺有大謬不然者。吹竽彈鋏，要庭呼闥，卽廝隸之役，弗旬於此矣；投機瞰隙，匿情更說，卽穿窬之跡，弗垢於此矣；摺體伏溺，希旨承顏，卽妾婦之容，弗媿於此矣。夫三者，至賤辱也，至亡行也，而士乃甘心焉，試之以七尺之軀，何也？彼見夫左繩右墨者之擯於時，而高議闊談者足以踞要樞也；彼見夫廉貞
translation_en: …to the point of being like birds, beasts, or barbarian captives who cannot be counted as possessing human reason, who among them would not cleanse, polish, and refine themselves so as not to be cast out from the ranks of gentlemen and scholars? Therefore, at that time, scholars held themselves in very high regard, and the world looked upon scholars with great veneration. When they composed their countenances, it was to set forth ritual propriety; when they restrained their steps, it was to tread the path of righteousness; and when they were cautiously attentive to laws, institutions, instructions, and ordinances, it was to make clear that they had superiors and dared not act on their own authority. An ancient once said, "To take being blameless as holding high rank, and to delight oneself in purity and integrity." It was for this reason that the scholars of the Zhou were esteemed. When it came to the Qin, however, it was not so. They dismissed Confucian learning, exalted hegemonic statecraft, and prized the taking of enemy heads in battle. Practitioners of vertical and horizontal alliances galloped ahead, those skilled incalculating others' minds were employed, those who checked whether their tongues were still intact advanced, and those who bound their feet in hesitation retreated. Consequently, all scholars bent on功名 (merit and fame) wagged their lips and swung their arms, winning the posts of ministers and chancellors through a moment's standing conversation. How could their momentum and influence at the time not be dazzling? Yet if one calmly examines the arts by which they operated, one finds them utterly perverse and wrong. Playing the reed pipe or tapping the sword hilt, intercepting patrons in courtyards and shouting at palace gates—even the toil of menial servants and lackeys is not more base [?] than this. Seizing opportunities and spying out crevices, concealing one's true feelings and shifting one's arguments—even the tracks of burglars boring through walls are not more sordid than this. Folding one's body and prostrating oneself in filth, currying favor with a ruler's intentions and catering to his countenance—even the demeanor of concubines and wives is not more shameful than this. Now, these three things are the height of baseness and disgrace, the extreme of conduct devoid of moral principle; yet scholars willingly indulged in them, putting their own seven-foot frames to the test—why was this? It was because they saw that those who held strictly to plumb-line and ink-cord were rejected by the age, whereas those who indulged in lofty, grandiose talk were able to occupy pivotal positions of power; they saw that the incorrupt, pure,…

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
直亮者之背於俗而淟涊詭隨者足以營
尊臚也教弛而法頹風夷而習敝威之所
不懾而令之所不格也則靡靡嚮風而爭
趨下矣昔人有言所治愈下得車愈多夫
秦之士所為桀驁橫恣者是得車多也其
治下矣亦烏足貴哉若廼兩漢之興其初
皆英君喆后一時功名節義之士雲合嚮
應若良平若耿鄧靡不展寀錯事策勛爍
譽蓋斌斌創業藎臣中興碩輔也洎乎晚
===
節末路浸淫敗壞不可收拾新莽一起而
頌功德者盈廷填闕即學如子雲尚為文
以美之為後世大詬其僅守箕山之節如
薛方者已稱希奇寥曠矣陳蕃竇武輩舉
事一不當駢首就僇於閹寺之手而顧廚
俊及諸君子亦以區區懸標張幟自取刑
錮是何嚮者慕用之誠後相誖之鑿也二
者皆譏而說者謂穢行不如立名長諛不
如抗節兩京之俗不能不置進讓焉儻亦
punctuated: 直亮者之背於俗，而淟涊詭隨者足以營尊臚也。教弛而法頹，風夷而習敝，威之所不懾，而令之所不格也，則靡靡嚮風而爭趨下矣。昔人有言：「所治愈下，得車愈多。」夫秦之士所為桀驁橫恣者，是得車多也；其治下矣，亦烏足貴哉？若廼兩漢之興，其初皆英君喆后，一時功名節義之士，雲合嚮應。若良、平，若耿、鄧，靡不展寀錯事，策勛爍譽，蓋斌斌創業藎臣、中興碩輔也。洎乎晚節末路，浸淫敗壞，不可收拾。新莽一起，而頌功德者盈廷填闕，即學如子雲，尚為文以美之，為後世大詬；其僅守箕山之節如薛方者，已稱希奇寥曠矣。陳蕃、竇武輩，舉事一不當，駢首就僇於閹寺之手；而顧、廚、俊、及諸君子，亦以區區懸標張幟，自取刑錮。是何嚮者慕用之誠，後相誖之鑿也？二者皆譏，而說者謂穢行不如立名，長諛不如抗節，兩京之俗不能不置進讓焉，儻亦
translation_en: … the upright and trustworthy are at odds with popular custom, while the filthy and deceitfully compliant are able to secure high rank and rich stipends. When moral instruction relaxes and the laws decay, when customs decline and habits grow corrupt—where neither authority can overawe nor decrees can reform—then people yield spinelessly to the prevailing wind and vie to sink ever lower. A person of old had a saying: "The lower the level of the cure, the more carriages the physician receives." Now, the reason the scholars of the Warring States and Qin were so unruly and unbridled is that they were getting "more carriages"; the governance was of the lowest sort, so how could it be worth valuing? As for the rise of the Two Han dynasties, at the outset of each there were heroic rulers and wise sovereigns, and in those moments men of merit, reputation, integrity, and righteousness gathered like clouds and responded like echoes. Men such as Zhang Liang 張良 and Chen Ping 陳平, or Geng Yan 耿弇 and Deng Yu 鄧禹, without exception displayed their talents and managed affairs, inscribing their merits and shining in renown; they were truly the resplendent, devoted ministers of a dynastic founding and the great辅佐 (assistants) of a restoration. Yet when each dynasty reached its declining years and final stretch, it became gradually steeped in corruption beyond all remedy. Once Wang Mang 王莽 of the Xin dynasty arose, those who sang the praises of his功德 (merit and virtue) filled the court and crowded the palace gates. Even someone as learned as Yang Xiong 揚雄 (Ziyun 子雲) wrote an essay to eulogize him, incurring great disgrace for posterity; while one who merely kept to the integrity of Mount Ji, such as Xue Fang 薛方, was already hailed as rare and extraordinarily aloof. As for men like Chen Fan 陳蕃 and Dou Wu 竇武, once their undertaking went awry, they were executed side by side at the hands of the eunuchs; and the worthy gentlemen known as the "Gu, Chu, Jun, and Ji" (顧、廚、俊、及) likewise brought punishment and proscription upon themselves merely by holding up banners and setting up standards of reputation. Why was there such sincere eagerness to employ worthy men in the beginning, and such jarring contradiction in the end? Both dynasties are subject to criticism, yet commentators say that sullying one's conduct is not as good as establishing a reputation, and practicing flattery is not as good as upholding integrity; thus, between the customs of the Two Capitals (Western and Eastern Han), one cannot help ranking one above the other. Perhaps it is also…

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
愚故竊有虞乎今之為士者也峩冠緩帶
俯仰傴僂託之乎儒雅尋章摘句誦繁記
醜託之乎弘博屏禮弃知出入恣睢託之
乎夷曠違世陸沈避地獨竄託之乎孤高
脩生葆真飡氣服道託之乎練要結倫交
黨感分遺身託之乎奇節褒言竅論不可
方物託之乎幼眇擊跽拳曲從臾承望託
之乎恭和若是者教之所去俗之所取也
法之所禁時之所勸也名相矛也實相詭
===
也而無所定雖十文武弗能理也夫表樹
於途則人亡弗趨焉鵠設於前則人亡弗
貫焉故聖王立國必有以端表而正鵠是
以振其靡而防其微審其所以取而靳其
所以予昔者越王將復吳而試其教燔臺
而鼓之使民赴火者賞在火也臨江而鼓
之使人赴水者賞在水也臨戰而使人絕
脰刳腹而無顧心者賞在兵也若令與袖
手裹足之夫同類而並賞之則士寧有出
punctuated: 愚故竊有虞乎今之為士者也。峩冠緩帶，俯仰傴僂，託之乎儒雅；尋章摘句，誦繁記醜，託之乎弘博；屏禮弃知，出入恣睢，託之乎夷曠；違世陸沈，避地獨竄，託之乎孤高；脩生葆真，飡氣服道，託之乎練要；結倫交黨，感分遺身，託之乎奇節；褒言竅論，不可方物，託之乎幼眇；擊跽拳曲，從臾承望，託之乎恭和。若是者，教之所去，俗之所取也；法之所禁，時之所勸也。名相矛也，實相詭也，而無所定，雖十文、武弗能理也。夫表樹於途，則人亡弗趨焉；鵠設於前，則人亡弗貫焉。故聖王立國，必有以端表而正鵠，是以振其靡而防其微，審其所以取而靳其所以予。昔者，越王將復吳而試其教：燔臺而鼓之，使民赴火者，賞在火也；臨江而鼓之，使人赴水者，賞在水也；臨戰而使人絕脰刳腹而無顧心者，賞在兵也。若令與袖手裹足之夫同類而並賞之，則士寧有出
translation_en: I therefore privately harbor anxieties regarding the scholars of today. Wearing tall caps and loose sashes, bowing and stooping with every movement, they pass this off as Confucian elegance; hunting down passages and plucking out phrases, reciting prolixities and memorizing oddities, they pass this off as broad erudition; casting aside ritual and discarding wisdom, going in and out with unbridled wilfulness, they pass this off as serene open-mindedness; turning away from the world to sink into obscurity, fleeing society to hide in solitude, they pass this off as solitary loftiness; cultivating life and preserving primal genuineness, imbibing vital breath and practicing the Dao, they pass this off as mastering the essentials; forming cliques and joining factions, moved by personal obligation to cast away their lives, they pass this off as extraordinary integrity; indulging in grandiose talk and specious arguments [?] that cannot be pinned down, they pass this off as subtle profundity; kneeling with outstretched arms and curling up submissively, flattering and catering to others' wishes, they pass this off as respectful harmony. Practices such as these are what moral instruction rejects, yet what popular custom adopts; what the law forbids, yet what the age encourages. Names contradict one another and realities belie one another, without anything being fixed—even if there were ten King Wens and King Wus, they could not bring order to it. Now, when a signpost is erected along the road, there is no one who does not hasten toward it; when a target is set up in front, there is no one who does not aim to pierce it. Therefore, when the sage kings established the state, they necessarily had the means to straighten the signpost and align the target; thereby they roused the decadent and guarded against incipient faults, carefully examining what they selected and being sparing with what they bestowed. In antiquity, when the King of Yue was about to take revenge on Wu and tested his instruction: he set fire to a terrace and beat the drums, making the people rush into the fire, because the reward lay in the fire; he approached the river and beat the drums, making men plunge into the water, because the reward lay in the water; and on the verge of battle, he made men sever their necks and slit their bellies without a backward glance, because the reward lay in warfare. If he had instead grouped them together with men who kept their hands in their sleeves and their feet bound, rewarding them all alike, then how would warriors ever have come forth…

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
者則鄕所謂頑冥顓蒙無人理者也必不
然矣區區東京之俗其敝也激西京之俗
其失也隨已無足尚又何秦之足云哉昔
者孟氏有言待文王而後興者凡民也若
夫豪傑之士雖無文王猶興夫執事所稱
者凡民之槩也非所以爲豪傑論也士生
明時沐
聖澤至有化之而不速肖風之而不響應則幾
無行矣愚不佞請以文王之化爲
===
聖世頌以豪傑之志爲多士勗執事其謂此何
第五問
姜鏡
同考試官訓導龍批寛猛迭用若循環然子虞
任法之過而欲濟以寛大可謂識時務者
考試官敎諭程批詞旨愷切非苟言者
考試官敎諭周批雄文卓識足冠時髦
甞謂法者治之具也而非所以爲治也識
治者緣於不得已以立法而不任法以求
punctuated:
者，則鄕所謂頑冥顓蒙、無人理者也，必不然矣！區區東京之俗，其敝也激；西京之俗，其失也隨，已無足尚，又何秦之足云哉！昔者孟氏有言：「待文王而後興者，凡民也；若夫豪傑之士，雖無文王猶興。」夫執事所稱者，凡民之槩也，非所以爲豪傑論也。士生明時，沐聖澤，至有化之而不速肖，風之而不響應，則幾無行矣。愚不佞，請以文王之化爲聖世頌，以豪傑之志爲多士勗，執事其謂此何？

第五問
姜鏡
同考試官訓導龍批：寛猛迭用，若循環然。子虞任法之過，而欲濟以寛大，可謂識時務者。
考試官敎諭程批：詞旨愷切，非苟言者。
考試官敎諭周批：雄文卓識，足冠時髦。

甞謂法者，治之具也，而非所以爲治也。識治者，緣於不得已以立法，而不任法以求
translation_en:
… then they would be what I earlier called stubborn, benighted, ignorant, and devoid of human reason—which is surely not the case! As for the paltry customs of the Eastern Capital [Eastern Han], their flaw was extremity; as for the customs of the Western Capital [Western Han], their failing was compliance. Even these are not worth esteeming, so what is there to say of Qin? In the past, Mencius [Mengzi] said: "Those who wait for a King Wen before rising up are ordinary folk; as for outstanding scholars, even without a King Wen they still rise up." What Your Excellency has described is the general standard of ordinary folk, not a way to judge outstanding men. When scholars are born in an enlightened era and bathed in Sacred Grace, if it comes to the point that they are transformed yet do not quickly emulate the good, or are moved by moral wind yet do not respond like an echo, then they are nearly devoid of moral conduct. Unworthy though I am, I beg to praise this Sacred Era with the transforming influence of King Wen, and to exhort the many scholars with the aspiration of outstanding men. What does Your Excellency say to this?

Question Five
Jiang Jing 姜鏡
Comment by Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor Long 龍: "Lenience and severity are used in alternation, like a cycle. You worry about the excesses of relying on law and wish to temper them with寬大 (magnanimity); you may be called one who understands the affairs of the times."
Comment by Examiner and Instructor Cheng 程: "The words and purport are earnest and incisive; this is no careless utterance."
Comment by Examiner and Instructor Zhou 周: "Powerful prose and outstanding insight, worthy of crowning the talents of the age."

I have held that law is an instrument of governance, and not that whereby governance is achieved. Those who understand governance establish laws only out of necessity, and do not rely on laws alone to seek…

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
治斯得之矣夫緣於不得已以立法則法
簡法簡則人將諒吾之不得已而相率以
守其法於不墜任法以求治則法煩法煩
則人將飾貌以避吾之法而法愈窮故識
治者甚無樂乎其任法也今之求治者吾
惑焉踵故襲常見謂頹靡而不振旣飭其
法以爲一切整齊之具其効也至於釐敝
起廢臻綜覈之理矣顧求之不已意以是
法爲終始而欲純任之吾恐天下之人一
===
時雖束於其法而不獲逞其久也必至潰
敗决裂而不可收拾是不可不爲之圖也
請縱談之以復明問嘗考邃古之初上下
玄同相與結繩而用之甘其食美其服樂
其俗安其居形有動作心無好惡當此之
時號爲至治不知有所謂法也迨風會日
流淳樸漓散智巧繁興聖人於是乎人爲
之防事爲之制而法立焉爲之名位以辨
其上下爲之爵賞以旌其功伐爲之刑罰
punctuated: 治，斯得之矣。夫緣於不得已以立法，則法簡；法簡，則人將諒吾之不得已，而相率以守其法於不墜。任法以求治，則法煩；法煩，則人將飾貌以避吾之法，而法愈窮。故識治者，甚無樂乎其任法也。今之求治者，吾惑焉。踵故襲常，見謂頹靡而不振；旣飭其法以爲一切整齊之具，其効也至於釐敝起廢，臻綜覈之理矣。顧求之不已，意以是法爲終始而欲純任之，吾恐天下之人，一時雖束於其法而不獲逞，其久也必至潰敗决裂而不可收拾，是不可不爲之圖也。請縱談之，以復明問。嘗考邃古之初，上下玄同，相與結繩而用之。甘其食，美其服，樂其俗，安其居，形有動作，心無好惡。當此之時，號爲至治，不知有所謂法也。迨風會日流，淳樸漓散，智巧繁興，聖人於是乎人爲之防，事爲之制，而法立焉。爲之名位以辨其上下，爲之爵賞以旌其功伐，爲之刑罰
translation_en: … order—then one has grasped it. Now, when one establishes laws out of necessity, the laws are simple; when the laws are simple, people will understand our lack of alternatives and lead one another in observing the laws so that they do not fall into ruin. When one relies solely on laws to seek order, the laws become繁冗 (burdensome and numerous); when the laws are burdensome, people will put on false appearances to evade our laws, and the laws will become ever more exhausted. Therefore, those who understand governance take no pleasure at all in relying solely on laws. As for those who seek order today, I am perplexed by them. When people follow old routines and cleave to convention, it is criticized as decadent and uninspired; yet once the laws have been tightened to serve as a sweeping instrument of uniformity, the effect has indeed reached the point of clearing away abuses, reviving neglected practices, and attaining the principle of comprehensive verification. However, if one demands this endlessly, intending to make such laws the beginning and the end and wishing to rely purely upon them, I fear that although the people of the empire may be temporarily bound by these laws and unable to indulge themselves, in the long run things will inevitably collapse, rupture, and become impossible to mend. For this, we cannot fail to take precautions. Allow me to speak freely on this in reply to the sagely question. I have examined the beginning of remote antiquity, when superiors and inferiors were in mysterious harmony and used knotted cords in their dealings with one another. They relished their food, found beauty in their clothing, rejoiced in their customs, and felt secure in their dwellings; their bodies had movement and action, yet their minds had no likes or dislikes. At that time, it was called the ultimate order, and no one knew of anything called "law." When the currents of custom shifted day by day, simple honesty thinned and scattered, and cleverness and artifice arose in profusion, the sages thereupon instituted safeguards for people and regulations for affairs, and thus laws were established. They created titles and ranks to distinguish superiors and inferiors, created noble ranks and rewards to honor merit and achievement, created punishments and penalties…

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
以肅其淫慝爲之條教以啓其趨避爲之
號令以約其渙散爲之甲兵以誅其暴亂
皆法也亦皆天下之情所不得已者也聖
人緣於不得已以立法故無貴賤無賢愚
無遠邇莫不恃聖人之法以爲安若水火
寒暑之不可廢焉施之於階前而準之於
海表創之於一朝而垂之於億載繼體守
成之君相與安坐而守之視其法如神物
而不敢侮如天造地設而不敢易雖有謀
===
畧之佐智詐之士不得越法而恣意藉令
法久而弊生窒礙而難施用亦惟徐察其
弊之所在而剔除之酌利害之大小權得
失之輕重而微爲之損益不得因弊而遽
廢其法故法行而民安之當此之時雖有
法猶無法也而天下亦治人不得援法而
議聖人迨哲王旣遠邪說橫行於是人始
奮其私智挾其偏見離跂攘臂而高議廟
堂之上往往任法而求治甚且視聖人之
punctuated: 以肅其淫慝，爲之條教以啓其趨避，爲之號令以約其渙散，爲之甲兵以誅其暴亂。皆法也，亦皆天下之情所不得已者也。聖人緣於不得已以立法，故無貴賤，無賢愚，無遠邇，莫不恃聖人之法以爲安，若水火寒暑之不可廢焉。施之於階前，而準之於海表；創之於一朝，而垂之於億載。繼體守成之君，相與安坐而守之，視其法如神物而不敢侮，如天造地設而不敢易。雖有謀畧之佐、智詐之士，不得越法而恣意。藉令法久而弊生，窒礙而難施用，亦惟徐察其弊之所在而剔除之，酌利害之大小，權得失之輕重，而微爲之損益，不得因弊而遽廢其法。故法行而民安之。當此之時，雖有法猶無法也，而天下亦治，人不得援法而議聖人。迨哲王旣遠，邪說橫行，於是人始奮其私智，挾其偏見，離跂攘臂而高議廟堂之上，往往任法而求治，甚且視聖人之
translation_en: … to restrain their licentiousness and wickedness; they formulated itemized instructions to guide people in what to pursue and what to avoid; they instituted commands and orders to bind together what was scattered; and they created armor and weapons to punish violence and rebellion. All of these are laws, and all arose from what was unavoidable in the circumstances of the world. Because the sages established laws out of what was unavoidable, everyone—whether noble or base, worthy or foolish, far or near—relied on the laws of the sages for security, just as water and fire, or winter cold and summer heat, cannot be dispensed with. Implemented before the palace steps, they served as the standard beyond the seas; created in a single morning, they were handed down for a hundred million years. Rulers who succeeded to the throne and preserved the achievements of their predecessors sat in peace and maintained them, regarding these laws as sacred objects that they dared not treat with contempt, and as things fashioned by Heaven and set in place by Earth that they dared not alter. Even if there were resourceful aides or cunning and deceitful men, they could not overstep the laws and act willfully. Even supposing that after a long time abuses arose in the laws so that they became obstructed and difficult to apply, one would only calmly observe where the abuses lay and weed them out, weighing the magnitude of the benefits and harms, balancing the gravity of the gains and losses, and making slight reductions or additions; one could not hastily abolish the laws simply because of abuses. Therefore, the laws functioned and the people were at peace with them. At such times, although there were laws, it was as though there were no laws, and yet the world was well-governed, and no one could cite the laws to criticize the sages. When the wise kings were long gone and heretical doctrines ran rampant, people first began to exert their private cleverness and harbor biased views, standing on tiptoe with sleeves rolled up to engage in lofty debates in the imperial court. Again and again they relied on laws alone to seek order, going so far as to regard the sages'…

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
法爲闊略疎漏輒妄取而改易破壞之創
爲一切以就功名詳悉其科條繁縟其節
目使民耳目口鼻悉聽命於上而不獲自
適其性命之情吹毛而求疵洗垢而索瘢
法愈密而民愈不堪於是民亦出其詭僻
淫險之智惑上之視聽而逃於法之外以
與吾角天下乃始大壞識者見其然乃遂
倂聖人之法而追咎之故莊周之言曰焚
符破璽而民朴鄙剖斗折衡而民不爭殫
===
殘天下之聖法而後可與論議淮南王安
之言曰民知書而德衰知數而厚衰知券
契而信衰知機械而實衰夫二子之言驟
而聽之宜若可駭徐而察之無亦病後世
之法密而興懷邃古之初以洩其憤悶不
平之氣乎非謂盡捐法而可以治天下也
是故法簡者昌法繁者亡事碎者難繼政
寬者易從三代而後可僂指數也漢高帝
一豐沛匹夫耳提劍而平秦亂天下所以
punctuated: 法爲闊略疎漏，輒妄取而改易破壞之，創爲一切，以就功名。詳悉其科條，繁縟其節目，使民耳目口鼻悉聽命於上，而不獲自適其性命之情。吹毛而求疵，洗垢而索瘢。法愈密而民愈不堪，於是民亦出其詭僻淫險之智，惑上之視聽，而逃於法之外，以與吾角，天下乃始大壞。識者見其然，乃遂倂聖人之法而追咎之。故莊周之言曰：「焚符破璽，而民朴鄙；剖斗折衡，而民不爭；殫殘天下之聖法，而後可與論議。」淮南王安之言曰：「民知書而德衰，知數而厚衰，知券契而信衰，知機械而實衰。」夫二子之言，驟而聽之，宜若可駭；徐而察之，無亦病後世之法密，而興懷邃古之初，以洩其憤悶不平之氣乎？非謂盡捐法而可以治天下也。是故法簡者昌，法繁者亡；事碎者難繼，政寬者易從。三代而後，可僂指數也。漢高帝，一豐沛匹夫耳，提劍而平秦亂，天下所以
translation_en: … laws as overly broad and negligent, and arbitrarily took to altering and destroying them, contriving sweeping, expedient measures in order to achieve personal功名 (merit and fame). They made the statutory articles minute in detail and the sub-clauses繁縟 (elaborate and burdensome), causing the people's ears, eyes, mouths, and noses to be entirely at the command of their superiors, unable to find satisfaction in the natural dispositions of their lives. They blew apart the fur to look for blemishes and washed away the dirt to search for scars. The denser the laws became, the less the people could endure them; thereupon the people also brought forth their deceitful, perverse, licentious, and treacherous wits to confuse the sight and hearing of their superiors and escape outside the law in order to contend with us—and only then did the realm begin to fall into great ruin. When men of insight saw that it was so, they consequently went so far as to retroactively blame the laws of the sages along with the rest. Thus the words of Zhuang Zhou (莊周) say: "Burn the tallies and shatter the seals, and the people will be simple and unadorned; split the peck-measures and snap the steelyards, and the people will not wrangle; utterly destroy the sagely laws of the world, and only then can one discuss matters with the people." And the words of Liu An, Prince of Huainan (淮南王安), say: "When the people know writing, virtue declines; when they know calculation, generosity declines; when they know contracts and tallies, trustworthiness declines; when they know mechanical contrivances, genuineness declines." Now, if one listens to the words of these two masters abruptly, they may well seem shocking; yet if one examines them calmly, were they not simply aggrieved by the denseness of the laws of later ages, and thus stirred to yearn for the beginnings of remote antiquity as a way to vent their indignant and discontented spirit? They did not mean that one could cast aside all laws completely and thereby govern the world. Therefore, those whose laws are simple flourish, and those whose laws are繁 (numerous and complicated) perish; affairs that are fragmented are hard to sustain, and governance that is lenient is easy to follow. After the Three Dynasties, the examples can be counted on one's fingers. Emperor Gao of Han (漢高帝) was merely a commoner from Feng (豐) and Pei (沛); he took up his sword and pacified the chaos of Qin (秦), and the reason the world…

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
歸之如流者以其入關中約法三章悉除
秦苛法以與民更始此所以迄成帝業而
開漢四百年之基也唐高祖一太原留守
耳起兵而平隋亂天下所以應之如響者
以其克長安約法十二條悉除隋苛禁以
與民休息此所以旋履帝位而開唐三百
年之統也商鞅之相秦孝公也令民相收
司連坐告姦者與斬敵首同賞不告姦者
與降敵同罰於是百姓樂用諸侯親服獲
===
楚魏之師闢地千里非不足以強秦也而
秦以慘酷亡吳起之相楚悼王也明法審
令捐不急之官廢公族疎遠者以撫養戰
鬪之士於是南平百越北卻三晉西抗強
秦諸侯不敢窺兵於漢水非不足以勁楚
也而楚以刻覈危夫使民居處相司有罪
相覺於弭姦得矣然而傷和睦之俗構仇
讎之怨馴致亡秦君子不為也罷其冗官
廢其疎族於惜費得矣然而結功臣之怨
punctuated: 歸之如流者，以其入關中約法三章，悉除秦苛法，以與民更始。此所以迄成帝業，而開漢四百年之基也。唐高祖一太原留守耳，起兵而平隋亂，天下所以應之如響者，以其克長安約法十二條，悉除隋苛禁，以與民休息。此所以旋履帝位，而開唐三百年之統也。商鞅之相秦孝公也，令民相收司連坐，告姦者與斬敵首同賞，不告姦者與降敵同罰；於是百姓樂用，諸侯親服，獲楚、魏之師，闢地千里。非不足以強秦也，而秦以慘酷亡。吳起之相楚悼王也，明法審令，捐不急之官，廢公族疎遠者，以撫養戰鬪之士；於是南平百越，北卻三晉，西抗強秦，諸侯不敢窺兵於漢水。非不足以勁楚也，而楚以刻覈危。夫使民居處相司，有罪相覺，於弭姦得矣；然而傷和睦之俗，構仇讎之怨，馴致亡秦，君子不為也。罷其冗官，廢其疎族，於惜費得矣；然而結功臣之怨，
translation_en: … rallied to him like a flowing stream was that upon entering Guanzhong he agreed upon a code of laws in three articles, completely abolishing the harsh laws of Qin so as to make a fresh start with the people. This is how he ultimately achieved the imperial enterprise and laid the foundation for the four hundred years of the Han dynasty. Emperor Gaozu of Tang was merely a Regent of Taiyuan; when he raised troops to quell the disorders of the Sui, the reason the realm responded to him like an echo was that upon capturing Chang'an he agreed upon a code of laws in twelve articles, completely abolishing the harsh prohibitions of Sui so as to give the people rest and recuperation. This is how he soon ascended the imperial throne and inaugurated the three-hundred-year succession of the Tang dynasty. When Shang Yang 商鞅 served as counselor to Duke Xiao of Qin 秦孝公, he ordered the people to supervise one another in mutual surveillance and collective liability: those who reported evildoers were rewarded the same as those who decapitated an enemy, and those who failed to report evildoers were punished the same as those who surrendered to an enemy. Thereupon the common people were eager to be employed, the feudal lords submitted in allegiance, the armies of Chu and Wei were captured, and territory was expanded by a thousand li. It is not that this was insufficient to strengthen Qin, yet Qin perished through cruelty and ruthlessness. When Wu Qi 吳起 served as counselor to King Dao of Chu 楚悼王, he clarified the laws and scrutinized ordinances, eliminated non-urgent offices, and abolished the privileges of distant branches of the ruling clan in order to nurture and support fighting men. Thereupon in the south he pacified the Hundred Yue, in the north he repulsed the Three Jin, and in the west he resisted powerful Qin, so that the feudal lords dared not cast ambitious eyes upon the Han River with their troops. It is not that this was insufficient to make Chu formidable, yet Chu was imperiled through harshness and severity. Now, causing the people in their dwellings to watch over one another and expose one another's crimes succeeded in suppressing wickedness; yet it damaged the customs of harmony and concord, bred the grievances of feuds and enmity, and gradually led to the ruin of Qin—a gentleman would not do it. Dismissing superfluous officials and abolishing the privileges of distant kinsmen succeeded in sparing expenditures; yet it incurred the resentment of meritorious ministers…

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
失貴戚之心馴致危楚君子不道也故商
鞅吳起之立法天下之所謂善者也舉以
與漢唐二祖竝論則疎密有間矣然而秦
楚促而漢唐之祚長者何也蓋商鞅察於
刀筆之跡而昧致理之源也吳起習於行
陳之事而略廟勝之筭也皆所謂不量天
下之情得已而不已者也求治者鏡漢唐
之所以長與秦楚之所以促始可與論法
矣姑以近事證之
===
明自
太祖高皇帝肇造區夏忿元綱之不振稍以法
繩臣下號稱嚴明至其圖艱難以示
後嗣修女誡以肅
宮闈興學校以敦教化定律令以重民命而
蠲租之詔至十餘下則又未甞不依於寬
大也
成祖而後解網弛禁務在無爲以順天下延及
孝宗俗化益厚無論士庶卽蟲魚草木靡不得
punctuated:
失貴戚之心，馴致危楚，君子不道也。故商鞅、吳起之立法，天下之所謂善者也。舉以與漢、唐二祖竝論，則疎密有間矣。然而秦、楚促而漢、唐之祚長者，何也？蓋商鞅察於刀筆之跡，而昧致理之源也；吳起習於行陳之事，而略廟勝之筭也。皆所謂不量天下之情，得已而不已者也。求治者鏡漢、唐之所以長，與秦、楚之所以促，始可與論法矣。

姑以近事證之：明自太祖高皇帝肇造區夏，忿元綱之不振，稍以法繩臣下，號稱嚴明。至其圖艱難以示後嗣，修《女誡》以肅宮闈，興學校以敦教化，定律令以重民命，而蠲租之詔至十餘下，則又未甞不依於寬大也。成祖而後，解網弛禁，務在無爲，以順天下。延及孝宗，俗化益厚，無論士庶，卽蟲魚草木靡不得
translation_en:
… alienated the hearts of the noble relatives, gradually bringing Chu into peril—this is what a gentleman refuses to speak of. Therefore, the laws established by Shang Yang and Wu Qi are what the world calls skillful. Yet if we bring them up to compare side by side with those of the founding emperors of Han and Tang, there is a clear difference between looseness and strictness. Why is it, then, that Qin and Chu were short-lived while the reigns of Han and Tang were long-lasting? It is because Shang Yang was discerning in the minutiae of legal clericalism, yet blind to the source of achieving good governance; and Wu Qi was versed in the affairs of military formations, yet neglectful of the strategic calculations that secure victory in the ancestral temple. Both are examples of what is meant by failing to gauge the sentiments of the realm, and refusing to stop when one could have stopped. Only when those who seek good governance use as a mirror the reasons why Han and Tang lasted long and why Qin and Chu were cut short can one discuss law with them.

Let us tentatively verify this with recent events. Since Emperor Taizu Gaohuangdi of the Ming founded the realm of China, indignant at the laxity of Yuan dynasty governance, he somewhat restrained his officials and subjects with the law, and his rule was renowned as strict and clear. Yet when it came to illustrating past hardships to instruct his descendants, compiling the Admonitions for Women (Nüjie) to bring solemnity to the palace quarters, establishing schools to foster moral transformation through education, codifying statutes and ordinances to value the lives of the people, and issuing edicts remitting taxes more than ten times, he never failed to rely upon leniency and magnanimity. From Emperor Chengzu onward, the net of the law was loosened and prohibitions were relaxed, with the aim of practicing non-action so as to accord with the realm. Extending down to the reign of Emperor Xiaozong, customs and moral transformation grew ever more generous; not to mention scholars and commoners, even insects, fish, grasses, and trees—there was none that did not attain…

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
而謀之假賓客童僕爲間諜乘虛而暮擣
其廬子弟忿而不救發囷倒廩盡亡其財
而家落乃始悵然而悔之無及矣此非善
治家者也我
國家引四海而磐石之安於覆盂雖萬萬無
它慮然自頃南北之事亦巳見於有象愚
恐羣不逞之徒左睨右盻而議於後也竊
聞
廟堂之上亦旣洞燭天下之情矣誠一計度
===
其得巳者悉從而巳之不求治於法而求
治於心不求治於下而求治於上與其勞
之莫若逸之與其擾之莫若寧之一靜可
以制百動一默足以應百諾事有利於小
而害於大者巳之而弗舉也政有所得輕
而所失重者巳之而弗行也如此則遠近
之情自服意外之虞漸弭可以遠邁漢唐
之曆永絶秦楚之禍雖儕之邃古可矣夫
良醫之治病在腠理則治在腸胃則治在
punctuated: 而謀之，假賓客、童僕爲間諜，乘虛而暮擣其廬。子弟忿而不救，發囷倒廩，盡亡其財而家落，乃始悵然而悔之，無及矣。此非善治家者也。我國家引四海而磐石之，安於覆盂，雖萬萬無它慮，然自頃南北之事，亦巳見於有象，愚恐羣不逞之徒，左睨右盻而議於後也。竊聞廟堂之上，亦旣洞燭天下之情矣。誠一計度其得巳者，悉從而巳之。不求治於法而求治於心，不求治於下而求治於上；與其勞之，莫若逸之；與其擾之，莫若寧之。一靜可以制百動，一默足以應百諾。事有利於小而害於大者，巳之而弗舉也；政有所得輕而所失重者，巳之而弗行也。如此，則遠近之情自服，意外之虞漸弭，可以遠邁漢、唐之曆，永絶秦、楚之禍，雖儕之邃古可矣。夫良醫之治病，在腠理則治，在腸胃則治，在
translation_en: …and plot against him, using his guests and boy servants as spies, taking advantage of an unguarded moment to raid his dwelling at dusk. His sons and younger brothers, resentful, do not come to his rescue. The raiders open his round granaries and empty his square storehouses; he loses all his wealth and his family falls into ruin. Only then does he feel vexed and regretful, when it is too late. Such is not one who knows well how to manage a household. Our Dynasty embraces the Four Seas and sets them upon bedrock, more secure than an overturned bowl. Although there is utterly no cause for other anxieties, yet from recent events in the north and south, signs have already become visible. In my foolishness, I fear that bands of malcontents are casting sidelong glances left and right, scheming behind the scenes. I have humbly heard that those in the imperial court have already thoroughly discerned the conditions of the realm. If they would truly calculate which measures can be dispensed with and dispense with them all—seeking good governance not in laws, but in the mind; seeking good governance not from those below, but from those above. Rather than toiling the people, it is better to give them ease; rather than disturbing them, it is better to grant them tranquility. One stillness can control a hundred movements; one silence suffices to answer a hundred assents. When an undertaking brings a small benefit but a great harm, dispense with it and do not initiate it; when a policy yields a slight gain but a heavy loss, dispense with it and do not put it into practice. In this way, the sentiments of those far and near will naturally submit, and unexpected dangers will gradually subside. We may then far surpass the longevity of the Han and Tang dynasties, forever cut off the calamities of Qin and Chu, and even stand as the equal of remote antiquity. Now, when a skilled physician treats an illness, if it is in the pores and subcutaneous tissues, it can be cured; if it is in the intestines and stomach, it can be cured; if it is in…

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
膏肓則有望之而走耳治天下猶治病也
今二三碩輔執斗杓而斟酌元氣卽有腠
理腸胃之疾一加鍼灸湯液旋就愈矣何
膏肓之足慮也
punctuated: 膏肓，則有望之而走耳。治天下猶治病也。今二三碩輔，執斗杓而斟酌元氣，卽有腠理、腸胃之疾，一加鍼灸、湯液，旋就愈矣，何膏肓之足慮也！
translation_en: … the vital region between the heart and the diaphragm (gaohuang), then he can only look upon the patient and flee. Governing the empire is like treating an illness. Today, two or three great chief ministers hold the handle of the Northern Dipper and regulate the primordial vitality of the state. Even if there are ailments in the pores or in the intestines and stomach, as soon as acupuncture, moxibustion, and medicinal decoctions are applied, they are promptly cured; what need is there to worry about the illness reaching the vital region between the heart and the diaphragm?

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
明興遂擅海內大較今
國家歲所合南北直隸及十三
省之士試之南宮而以進於
明天子之庭者什二三焉端容嘗
遵錢塘登會稽及泝漢太史
公司馬氏所弔禹之遺烈其
所當山川之吐吞風氣之磅
===
礴亘斗牛薄虹霓非特古所
稱一都會而已也故嘗按吳
越之志公子札范蠡言偃以
來世多聞人即如今諸生所
挾冊以試于有司者言人人
殊端容間覆之其言冠裳則
似禹之南會諸侯而執玉帛
punctuated: 明興，遂擅海內。大較今國家歲所合南北直隸及十三省之士，試之南宮，而以進於明天子之庭者，什二三焉。端容嘗遵錢塘，登會稽，及泝漢太史公司馬氏所弔禹之遺烈，其所當山川之吐吞、風氣之磅礴，亘斗牛，薄虹霓，非特古所稱一都會而已也。故嘗按吳、越之志，公子札、范蠡、言偃以來，世多聞人。即如今諸生所挾冊以試于有司者，言人人殊。端容間覆之：其言冠裳，則似禹之南會諸侯，而執玉帛
translation_en: … With the rise of the Ming, it came to stand preeminent within the realm. Broadly speaking, in our dynasty today, of the scholars gathered periodically from the Northern and Southern Metropolitan Areas and the thirteen provinces to be examined in the Ministry of Rites and presented at the court of the enlightened Son of Heaven, two or three out of ten come from here. I, Duanrong, once traveled along the Qiantang River, ascended Mount Kuaiji, and traced back the surviving achievements of Yu the Great that the Han Grand Historian Sima Qian had paid tribute to. The surging and swallowing of its mountains and rivers and the majestic breadth of its vital energy span the constellations Dipper and Ox and brush against the rainbows—it is not merely what antiquity called a great metropolis and nothing more. Thus, when I examined the records of Wu and Yue, I saw that from the time of Prince Zha [Jizha], Fan Li, and Yan Yan [Ziyou] onward, every generation has produced famous men. Even among the scholars of today who bring their writing tablets to be examined by the authorities, each speaks with a distinct voice of his own. When I, Duanrong, took occasion to review them: those whose words are stately and ceremonious resemble Yu the Great assembling the feudal lords in the south, with those holding jade and silk…

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
者萬國其言鞭風叱霆精光
四射則似歐冶之干將莫耶
其言蒨麗青蔥則似西湖剡
曲其言澹宕縹緲則似雁宕
赤城其言滉漾無垠則又似
東望扶桑北眺碣石而鮫之
宮蜃之窟以相波濤焉猗與
===
美哉洋洋乎誠所謂大國之
風而諸士子之颺翔而雲蒸
於
朝者有以也雖然端容竊有一
焉玆諸生所言也卽古者詢
事考言之初也獨不曰乃言
底績已乎言也者文也仲尼
punctuated: 者萬國；其言鞭風叱霆、精光四射，則似歐冶之干將、莫耶；其言蒨麗青蔥，則似西湖、剡曲；其言澹宕縹緲，則似雁宕、赤城；其言滉漾無垠，則又似東望扶桑、北眺碣石，而鮫之宮、蜃之窟以相波濤焉。猗與美哉！洋洋乎誠所謂大國之風，而諸士子之颺翔而雲蒸於朝者有以也。雖然，端容竊有一焉：玆諸生所言也，卽古者詢事考言之初也，獨不曰「乃言底績」已乎？言也者，文也。仲尼
translation_en: … holding jade and silk numbered ten thousand states; those whose words whip the wind and rebuke the thunder, shooting forth brilliant light in all directions, resemble Ou Ye’s swords Ganjiang and Moye; those whose words are luxuriant, lovely, and verdantly lush resemble West Lake (Xihu) and the bends of the Shan River (Shanqu); those whose words are tranquil, unrestrained, and ethereally distant resemble Mount Yandang and Mount Chicheng; and those whose words are vast, surging, and boundless further resemble gazing east toward Fusang and looking north toward Mount Jieshi, where the palaces of sharks and the caverns of giant clams churn with the waves and billows. How admirable and splendid! Vast and grand indeed—truly what is called the air of a great state, and there is good reason why the scholars soar aloft and rise like clouds to the Court. Even so, I, Duanrong, venture to have one thought on this: what the candidates have set forth in words here is the very beginning of what the ancients called inquiring into affairs and examining words—yet was it not also said, “Your words can be carried out into concrete accomplishments”? Words are literary expression. Did Confucius (Zhongni) …

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
不云乎文莫吾猶人也迺若
績也者則所以體之心見諸
行事於以發之乎立
朝而莅官臨民焉也他不暇引
卽如我
國家劉公基章公溢葉公琛宋
公濂王公禕始以
===
帷幄訏謨文章典禮翊戴
高皇帝草昧之際者當與商之萊
朱周之閎夭等其他戡亂定
難身捍
社稷則于公謙仗節死事歔欷嗚
咽則方公孝孺孫公燧抗聲
直諫死且不避則章公綸張
punctuated: 不云乎：「文，莫吾猶人也。」迺若績也者，則所以體之心、見諸行事，於以發之乎立朝而莅官臨民焉也。他不暇引，卽如我國家劉公基、章公溢、葉公琛、宋公濂、王公禕，始以帷幄訏謨、文章典禮翊戴高皇帝草昧之際者，當與商之萊朱、周之閎夭等；其他戡亂定難、身捍社稷，則于公謙；仗節死事、歔欷嗚咽，則方公孝孺、孫公燧；抗聲直諫、死且不避，則章公綸、張
translation_en: …not say, "In letters, am I not perhaps equal to others?" As for actual achievements, however, they are what one embodies in the mind and manifests in practical affairs, thereby bringing them forth when standing at court, assuming office, and governing the people. Without taking time to cite examples from elsewhere, consider right here in our dynasty Lord Liu Ji 劉基, Lord Zhang Yi 章溢, Lord Ye Chen 葉琛, Lord Song Lian 宋濂, and Lord Wang Yi 王禕, who in the beginning assisted and supported the August High Emperor [Hongwu] amid the chaos of the founding through their grand counsels in the command tent and their literary writings and ritual institutions—they surely rank alongside Lai Zhu 萊朱 of the Shang and Hong Yao 閎夭 of the Zhou. As for others: in quelling rebellion and settling crises, defending the altars of state in person, there was Lord Yu Qian 于謙; in upholding integrity and dying for duty, moving people to sobs and sighs, there were Lord Fang Xiaoru 方孝孺 and Lord Sun Sui 孫燧; in raising their voices in forthright remonstrance and not shrinking even from death, there were Lord Zhang Lun 章綸 and [Lord] Zhang…

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
公寧正色率下大雅不羣則
商公輅謝公遷文經武緯超
曠百世則王公守仁抒忠發
姦彈壓中外則胡公世寧理
學淵懿領褒士林則章公懋
陳公選他名臣碩卿後先鱗
次屬望儒紳者不可勝數斯
===
皆吳越諸州郡之産先民之
考鏡也斯皆所謂考言而底
績而黃鐘大呂與日月俱遠
者也爾諸士子所沐
今天子嚮明之化十年于玆抑亦
深且遐矣得無上探公子札
范蠡而下之流風餘韻下按
punctuated: 公寧；正色率下、大雅不羣，則商公輅、謝公遷；文經武緯、超曠百世，則王公守仁；抒忠發姦、彈壓中外，則胡公世寧；理學淵懿、領褒士林，則章公懋、陳公選。他名臣碩卿，後先鱗次，屬望儒紳者，不可勝數。斯皆吳越諸州郡之産，先民之考鏡也；斯皆所謂考言而底績，而黃鐘大呂，與日月俱遠者也。爾諸士子所沐今天子嚮明之化，十年于玆，抑亦深且遐矣！得無上探公子札、范蠡而下之流風餘韻，下按
translation_en: … Master [Zhang] Ning 張寧; for leading subordinates with stern integrity and possessing refined elegance that stood out from the crowd, there were Master Shang Lu 商輅 and Master Xie Qian 謝遷; for weaving the warp of civil culture with the woof of military prowess, transcending a hundred generations, there was Master Wang Shouren 王守仁; for pouring forth loyalty to expose treachery and overawing both the court and the provinces, there was Master Hu Shining 胡世寧; for profound and virtuous Neo-Confucian learning that won the highest praise of the literati community, there were Master Zhang Mao 章懋 and Master Chen Xuan 陳選. Otherrenowned ministers and great statesmen, following one after another like fish scales and looked up to by Confucian gentry, are too numerous to count. All of these were born in the various prefectures and counties of Wu and Yue [Zhejiang], and serve as mirrors for instruction from our predecessors; all of these are what is meant by those whose words were examined and who achieved real results, and whose resonance—like the Yellow Bell and Great Tube pitch-pipes—endures as long as the sun and moon. You scholars have been bathed in the transforming influence of the present Son of Heaven's rule facing the light for ten years now—an influence that is indeed both deep and far-reaching! Could you fail, looking upward, to explore the lingering customs and echoes of Prince Zha 公子札 [Ji Zha], Fan Li 范蠡, and those who came after them, and looking downward, to examine …

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
今
國家劉公基宋公濂輩百年勝
述所相與銘旂常垂竹帛者
互爲烜爀熠燿已乎唐陸忠
宣公贄之知貢舉也得一昌
黎韓愈而唐之文崛起八代
之衰宋歐陽文忠公脩之知
===
貢舉也得一眉山蘇軾而宋
之士通經博古爲尚史官書
之於今播人耳目耿耿不磨
若昨日事茲則爾諸士子之
所以不負有司而於吳越之
山靈欻光而流潤也茲則御
史監試事者所以報稱
punctuated: 今國家劉公基、宋公濂輩百年勝述，所相與銘旂常、垂竹帛者，互爲烜爀熠燿已乎？唐陸忠宣公贄之知貢舉也，得一昌黎韓愈，而唐之文崛起八代之衰；宋歐陽文忠公脩之知貢舉也，得一眉山蘇軾，而宋之士通經博古爲尚。史官書之，於今播人耳目，耿耿不磨，若昨日事。茲則爾諸士子之所以不負有司，而於吳越之山靈欻光而流潤也；茲則御史監試事者所以報稱
translation_en: …the magnificent accounts over the centuries of such figures of our present dynasty as Master Liu Ji 劉基 and Master Song Lian 宋濂—those deeds inscribed together on royal banners and ceremonial tripods and handed down on bamboo and silk—so as to rival them in brilliance and splendor? When Master Lu Zhi 陸贄 (canonized Zhongxuan 忠宣) of the Tang served as Examiner of the tribute examinations, he obtained a single Han Yu 韓愈 of Changli 昌黎, and the literature of the Tang rose up from the decline of eight dynasties; when Master Ouyang Xiu 歐陽脩 (canonized Wenzhong 文忠) of the Song served as Examiner of the tribute examinations, he obtained a single Su Shi 蘇軾 of Meishan 眉山, and the scholars of the Song came to prize mastery of the Classics and broad knowledge of antiquity. Official historians recorded these events, and to this day they resound in people's eyes and ears, shining and indelible, as though they happened only yesterday. This, then, is how all you scholars will avoid disappointing the authorities and will suddenly shed light and spread luster upon the mountain spirits of Wu and Yue; this, then, is how the Censor supervising the examination affairs will fittingly repay…

title: 萬曆十年浙江鄉試錄
text:
明天子而端容與百執事亦稍稍
古者拔什得五之遺而少逭
臯戾也爾諸士子其謂然否
是爲序
江西吉安府廬陵縣儒學敎
諭程端容謹序
punctuated:
明天子，而端容與百執事亦稍稍古者拔什得五之遺，而少逭臯戾也。爾諸士子其謂然否？是爲序。
江西吉安府廬陵縣儒學敎諭程端容謹序。
translation_en:
…our enlightened Son of Heaven, while I, Duanrong, and all the officiating functionaries may also in some small measure follow the ancient legacy of "selecting ten and obtaining five" [worthy men], thereby somewhat escaping blame and transgression. You scholars, do you consider this to be so or not? This serves as the preface.
Respectfully prefaced by Cheng Duanrong 程端容, Confucian School Instructor (Ruxue Jiaoyu) of Luling County, Ji'an Prefecture, Jiangxi.
